### <term>Nâga</term> (*Sanskrit*).
Literally “Serpent.” In the Indian pantheon, it is the name of the serpent or dragon spirits and the inhabitants of <term>*Pâtâla*</term> (hell). But since <term>*Pâtâla*</term> means the *antipodes* and was the name given to America by the ancients (who knew and visited that continent before Europe had ever heard of it), the term is probably related to the Mexican <term>*Nagals*</term>, the modern-day sorcerers and medicine men. The <term>Nagas</term> are the Burmese <term>*Nats*</term>—serpent-gods or “dragon demons.” In <term>esotericism</term>, however, and as previously stated, this is a nickname for “wise men” or adepts. In China and Tibet, the “dragons” are regarded as the tutelary deities of the world and of various spots on the earth; the word is explained as meaning adepts, yogis, and *narjols* [saints]. The term simply refers to their great knowledge and wisdom. This is also proven in the ancient <term>*Sûtras*</term> and the biographies of <term>Buddha</term>. The <term>Nâga</term> is always a wise man endowed with extraordinary magic powers, whether in South and Central America, India, Chaldea, or ancient Egypt. In China, the “worship” of the <term>Nâgas</term> was widespread, and it has become even more pronounced since <term>*Nâgârjuna*</term> (literally the “great <term>Nâga</term>” or “great adept”), the fourteenth <term>Buddhist</term> patriarch, visited China. The “<term>Nâgas</term>” are regarded by the Chinese as the “tutelary spirits or gods of the five regions—the four points of the compass and the center—and as the guardians of the five lakes and four oceans” (*Eitel*). When traced to its origin and translated esoterically, this means that the five continents and their five root-races had always been under the guardianship of “terrestrial deities,” that is, <term>wise adepts</term>. The tradition that <term>Nâgas</term> washed <term>Gautama Buddha</term> at his birth, protected him, and guarded the relics of his body after death, further indicates that the <term>Nâgas</term> were merely wise men, <term>Arhats</term>, and not monsters or dragons. This is also supported by the countless stories of the conversion of <term>Nâgas</term> to <term>Buddhism</term>. For example, the <term>Nâga</term> of a lake in a forest near <term>*Râjagriha*</term> and many other “dragons” were converted by <term>Buddha</term> to the Good Law.

### <term>Nâgadwîpa</term> (*Sanskrit*).
Literally, “the island of the dragons”; it is one of the seven divisions of <term>*Bhâratavarsha*</term> (modern India) according to the <term>*Purânas*</term>. No evidence remains regarding who the <term>Nâgas</term> were—though they were a historical people—but the favorite theory is that they were a <term>Scythic</term> race. However, there is no proof of this. Legend says that when the <term>Brahmans</term> invaded India, they “found a race of wise men, half-gods and half-demons,” who were the teachers of other races and became the instructors of both the <term>Hindus</term> and the <term>Brahmans</term> themselves. <term>*Nagpur*</term> is rightfully believed to be the surviving remnant of <term>Nâgadwîpa</term>. Now, <term>*Nagpur*</term> is essentially in <term>*Râjputana*</term>, near <term>*Oodeypore*</term>, <term>*Ajmere*</term>, etc. And is it not well known that there was once a time when <term>Brahmans</term> went to learn secret wis[dom]...

**Nagal.** The title of the chief sorcerer or "medicine man" of some tribes of Mexican Indians. These individuals always keep a *daemon* or god in the shape of a serpent—and sometimes another sacred animal—which is said to inspire them.

**Nagarajas** (*Sk.*). The usual name given to all the supposed "guardian spirits" of lakes and rivers, meaning literally "Dragon Kings." All of these are shown in the Buddhist chronicles as having been converted to the Buddhist monastic life—that is, becoming Arhats from the Yogis they were before.

**Nagarjuna** (*Sk.*). An Arhat and hermit (a native of Western India) converted to Buddhism by Kapimala; he was the fourteenth Patriarch and is now regarded as a Bodhisattva-Nirmanakaya. He was famous for his dialectical subtlety in metaphysical arguments, was the first teacher of the Amitabha doctrine, and a representative of the Mahayana School. Viewed as the greatest philosopher of the Buddhists, he was referred to as "one of the four suns that illuminate the world." He was born in 223 B.C. and, after his conversion, went to China and in turn converted the whole country to Buddhism.

**Nagkon Wat** (*Siam.*). Imposing ruins in the province of Siem Reap (Eastern Siam), if they can even be called ruins. It is an abandoned building of most gigantic dimensions which, together with the great temple of Angkor Thom, are the best-preserved relics of the past in all Asia. After the Pyramids, this is the most occult building in the whole world. Of an oblong form, it is 796 feet long and 588 feet wide, built entirely of stone, including the roof, but *without cement* like the pyramids of Giza; the stones fit so closely that the joints are even now hardly visible. It has a central pagoda 250 feet high from the first floor and four smaller pagodas at the four corners, each about 175 feet high. In the words of a traveler (Frank Vincent, *The Land of the White Elephant*, p. 209): "In style and beauty of architecture, solidity of construction, and magnificent and elaborate carving and sculpture, the great Nagkon Wat has no superior—certainly no rival—standing today." (See *Isis Unveiled*, Vol. 1. pp. 561-566.)

**Nahash** (*Heb.*). "The Deprived"; the Evil One or the Serpent, according to the Western Kabbalists.

**Nahbkoon** (*Eg.*). The god who unites the "doubles," a mystical term referring to the human disembodied "principles."

**Naimittika** (*Sk.*). Occasional or incidental; used for one of the four kinds of Pralayas (See "Pralaya").

**Nain** (*Scand.*). The "Dwarf of Death."

**Najo** (*Hind.*). A witch or sorceress.

**Nakshatra** (*Sk.*). Lunar asterisms.

**Namah** (*Sk.*). In Pali, *Namo*. The first word of a daily invocation among Buddhists, meaning “I humbly trust,” or “adore,” or “acknowledge” the Lord; such as: “*Namo tasso Bhagovato Arhato*” etc., addressed to Lord Buddha. The priests are called “Masters of Namah”—both Buddhist and Taoist—because this word is used in liturgy and prayers, in the invocation of the *Triratna* (q.v.), and with a slight change in the occult incantations to the *Bodhisattvas* and *Nirmânakâyas*.

**Nanda** (*Sk.*). One of the Kings of Magadha (whose dynasty was overthrown by Chandragupta, q.v.).

**Nandi** (*Sk.*). The sacred white bull of Siva and his *Vâhan* (Vehicle).

**Nanna** (*Scand.*). The beautiful bride of Baldur, who fought with the blind Hodur (“he who rules over darkness”) and received his death from the latter through magic art. Baldur is the personification of Day, Hodur of Night, and the lovely Nanna of Dawn.

**Nannak** (*Chald.*), also *Nânar* and *Sin*. A name of the moon; said to be the son of *Muli* (the older Bel) and the Sun in later mythology. In the earliest mythology, the Moon is far older than the Sun.

**Nara** (*Sk.*). “Man,” the original, eternal man.

**Nârâ** (*Sk.*). The waters of Space, or the Great Deep, from which comes the name of *Nârâyana* or Vishnu.

**Nara Sinha** (*Sk.*). Literally, “Man-lion”; an Avatar of Vishnu.

**Nârada** (*Sk.*). One of the Seven great Rishis, a Son of Brahmâ. This “Progenitor” is one of the most mysterious personages in the Brahmanical sacred symbology. Esoterically, Nârada is the Ruler of events during various Karmic cycles, and the personification, in a certain sense, of the great human cycle; a Dhyan Chohan. He plays a major role in Brahmanism, which attributes to him some of the most occult hymns in the *Rig Veda*, in which sacred work he is described as being “of the *Kanwa family*.” He is called Deva-Brahmâ, but as such, he has a character distinct from the one he assumes on earth—or Pâtâla. Daksha cursed him for his interference with his 5,000 and 10,000 sons, whom he persuaded to remain Yogis and celibates, to be reborn time after time on this earth (*Mahâbhârata*). But this is an allegory. He was the inventor of the *Vina*, a type of lute, and a great “lawgiver.” The story is too long to be provided here.

**Nâraka** (*Sk.*). In the popular conception, a hell, a “prison under the earth.” The hot and cold hells, each eight in number, are simply emblems of the globe of our sevenfold chain, with the addition of the “eighth sphere” supposed to be located in the moon. This is a transparent *blind* <note>In occultism, a "blind" is a deliberate veil or distraction that hides a deeper truth.</note>, as these “hells” are called *vivifying hells* because, as explained, any being dying in one is immediately born in the second, then in the third, and so on; life lasts in each for 500 years (a *blind* on the number of cycles and reincarnations). As these hells constitute one of the six *gâti* (conditions of sentient existence), and as people are said

**Narayana** (*Sk*.). The “mover on the Waters” of space; a title of <term>Vishnu</term>, in his aspect of the <term>Holy Spirit</term>, moving on the Waters of Creation. (See *Manu*, Book II.) In esoteric symbolism, it represents the primeval manifestation of the <term>life-principle</term>, spreading through infinite Space.

**Nargal** (*Chald*.). The Chaldean and Assyrian chiefs of the <term>Magi</term> (*Rab Mag*).

**Narjol** (*Tib*.). A <term>Saint</term>; a glorified <term>Adept</term>.

**Nâros** or *Neros* (*Heb*.). A cycle, which Orientalists describe as consisting of 600 years. But what kind of years? There were three kinds of <term>Neros</term>: the greater, the middle, and the lesser. It is only the latter cycle that lasted 600 years. (See “Neros”.)

**Nâstika** (*Sk*.). An <term>Atheist</term>, or rather one who does not worship or recognize the gods and idols.

**Nâth** (*Sk*.). A Lord; used for both gods and men; a title added to the first name of men and things, such as <term>Badrinath</term> (lord of mountains), a famous place of pilgrimage; and <term>Gopinath</term> (lord of the shepherdesses), used for <term>Krishna</term>.

**Nava Nidhi** (*Sk*.). *Lit*., “the nine Jewels”; a culmination of spiritual development in <term>mysticism</term>.

**Nazar** (*Heb*.). One who is “set apart”; a temporary monastic class of celibates mentioned in the <term>Old Testament</term> who did not marry, nor did they drink wine during the time of their vow. They wore their hair long, cutting it only at their initiation. <term>Paul</term> must have belonged to this class of <term>Initiates</term>, for he tells the *Galatians* (i. 15) himself that he was *separated* or “set apart” from the moment of his birth; and that he had his hair cut at <term>Cenchrea</term> because “he had a vow” (*Acts* xviii. 18)—that is, he had been initiated as a <term>Nazar</term>. After this, he became a “master-builder” (1 *Corinth*. iii. 10). <term>Joseph</term> is called a <term>Nazar</term> (*Gen*. xlix. 26). <term>Samson</term> and <term>Samuel</term> were also <term>Nazars</term>, as were many others.

**Nazarenes** (*Heb*.). The same as the <term>St. John Christians</term>; also called the <term>Mendæans</term> or <term>Sabeans</term>. Those <term>Nazarenes</term> who left <term>Galilee</term> several hundred years ago and settled in <term>Syria</term>, east of <term>Mount Lebanon</term>, also call themselves <term>Galileans</term>; though they designate <term>Christ</term> as “a false <term>Messiah</term>” and recognize only <term>St. John the Baptist</term>, whom they call the “<term>Great Nazar</term>”. **Neilos** (*Gr.*). The river <term>Nile</term>; also a god.

**Neocoros** (*Gr.*). Among the Greeks, the guardian of a <term>Temple</term>.

### Neo-Platonism.
Literally, "The new <term>Platonism</term>" or <term>Platonic School</term>. An eclectic pantheistic school of philosophy founded in <term>Alexandria</term> by <term>Ammonius Saccas</term>, of which his disciple <term>Plotinus</term> was the head (A.D. 189-270). It sought to reconcile <term>Platonic</term> teachings and the <term>Aristotelian</term> system with oriental <term>Theosophy</term>. Its chief occupation was pure spiritual philosophy, metaphysics, and mysticism. <term>Theurgy</term> was introduced toward its later years. It was the ultimate effort of high intelligences to check the ever-increasing ignorant superstition and blind faith of the times; it was the last product of <term>Greek philosophy</term>, which was finally crushed and put to death by brute force.

### Nephesh Chia
(<term>Kabbalah</term>). Animal or living Soul.

### Nephesh
(<term>Hebrew</term>). Breath of life. *Anima, Mens, Vita, Appetites*. This term is used very loosely in the Bible. It generally means <term>Prana</term> "life"; in the <term>Kabbalah</term> it represents the animal passions and the animal Soul. <note>w.w.w.</note> Therefore, as maintained in theosophical teachings, <term>Nephesh</term> is the synonym of the <term>Prâna-Kâmic Principle</term>, or the vital animal Soul in man. <note>H. **Nergal** (*Chald.*). On the Assyrian tablets, he is described as the “giant king of war, lord of the city of Cutha.” It is also the Hebrew name for the planet Mars, associated invariably with bad luck and danger. Nergal-Mars is the “shedder of blood.” In occult astrology, it is less malevolent than Saturn, but is more active in its associations with men and its influence on them.

**Neros** (*Heb.*). As shown by the late E. V. Kenealy, this “Naronic Cycle” was a mystery—a true “secret of God.” To disclose this during the prevalence of the religious mysteries and the authority of the priests meant death. The learned author seemed to take it for granted that the Neros lasted for 600 years, but he was mistaken. (See “Nâros.”) Nor were the establishment of the Mysteries and the rites of Initiation due merely to the necessity of perpetuating the knowledge of the true meaning of the Naros and keeping this cycle secret from the profane; for the Mysteries are as old as the human race itself, and there were far more important secrets to veil than the figures of any cycle. (See “Neophyte” and “I. H. S.”; also “Nâros.”) The mystery of 666, the so-called “number of the great heart,” is far better represented by the Tau and the *Resh* than by 600.

**Nerthus** (*Old Saxon*). The goddess of the earth, love, and beauty among the ancient Germans; the same as the Scandinavian Freya or Frigga. Tacitus mentions the great honors paid to Nerthus when her idol was carried on a carriage in triumph through several districts.

**Neshamah** (*Heb.*). Soul, *anima*, *breath*. In the Kabbalah, as taught in the Rosicrucian order, it is one of the three highest essences of the Human Soul, corresponding to the *Sephira Binah*. [w.w.w.]

**Nesku** or **Nusku** (*Chald.*). Is described in the Assyrian tablets as the “holder of the golden scepter, the lofty god.”

**Netzach** (*Heb.*). “Victory.” The seventh of the Ten Sephiroth, a masculine active potency. [w.w.w.]

**Nidâna** (*Sk.*). The twelve causes of existence, or a chain of causation—a “linking together of cause and effect in the whole range of existence through twelve links.” This is the fundamental dogma of Buddhist thought, “the understanding of which solves the riddle of life, revealing the insanity of existence and preparing the mind for Nirvâna” (Eitel’s *Sanskrit Chinese Dictionary*). (2) *Jâmarana*, or decrepitude and death, following the maturity of the *Skandhas* (see entry). (3) *Bhava*, the Karmic agent which leads every new sentient being to be

**Nidhi** (*Sk.*). A treasure. Nine treasures belonging to the god Kuvera—the Vedic Satan—each treasure being under the guardianship of a demon; these are personified and are the objects of worship of the Tantrikas.

**Nidhogg** (*Scand.*). The “Mundane” Serpent.

**Nidra** (*Sk.*). Sleep. Also the female form of Brahmâ.

**Niflheim** (*Scand.*). The cold Hell in the *Edda*. A place of eternal unconsciousness and inactivity. (See *The Secret Doctrine*, Vol. II., p. 245).

**Night of Brahmâ**. The period between the dissolution and the active life of the Universe which is called, in contrast, the “Day of Brahmâ”.

**Nilakantha** (*Sk.*). A name of Siva meaning “blue-throated”. This is said to have been the result of poison administered to the god.

**Nile-God** (*Eg.*). Represented by a wooden image of the river god receiving honors in gratitude for the bounties its waters afford the country. There was a “celestial” Nile, called in the Ritual *Nen-naou* or “primordial waters”; and a terrestrial Nile, worshipped at *Nilopolis* and *Hapimoo*. The latter was represented as an androgynous being with a beard and breasts, and a fat blue face; green limbs and a reddish body. At the approach of the yearly inundation, the image was carried from one place to another in a solemn procession.

**Nimbus** (*Lat.*). The aureole around the heads of the Christ and Saints in Greek and Roman <note>The original text uses "Romish," a historical term for Roman Catholic.</note> Churches is of Eastern origin. As every Orientalist knows, Buddha is described as having his head surrounded with shining glory six cubits in width; and, as shown by Hardy (*Eastern Monachism*), “his principal disciples are represented by the native painters as having a similar mark of eminence”. In China, Tibet, and Japan, the heads of the saints are always surrounded with a nimbus.

**Nimitta** (*Sk.*). 1. An inner illumination developed by the practice of meditation. 2. The efficient spiritual cause, as contrasted with *Upadâna*, the material cause, in Vedânta philosophy. See also *Pradhâna* in Sânkhya philosophy.

**Nine.** The “Kabbalah of the Nine Chambers” is a form of secret writing in cipher that originated with the Hebrew Rabbis and has been used by several societies for the purpose of concealment; notably, some grades of the Freemasons have adopted it. A figure is drawn of two horizontal parallel lines and two vertical parallel lines crossing them; this process forms nine chambers, the center one being a simple square and the others being either two- or three-sided figures. These are allotted to various letters in any order that is agreed upon. There is also a Kabbalistic attribution of the ten Sephiroth to these nine chambers, but this is not published. <note>w.w.w.</note>

**Nirguna** (*Sk.*). Negative attribute; unbound, or without *Gunas* (attributes)—that is, that which is devoid of all qualities, the opposite of Saguna, which has attributes (*Secret Doctrine*, II. 95). For example, Parabrahman is Nirguna; Brahmâ is Saguna. Nirguna is a term that indicates the impersonality of the subject being discussed.

**Nirmânakâya** (*Sk.*). Something entirely different in esoteric philosophy from the popular meaning attached to it and from the fancies of the Orientalists. Some call the *Nirmânakâya* body “Nirvâna with remains” (Schlagintweit, etc.), probably on the supposition that it is a kind of Nirvânic condition during which consciousness and form are retained. Others say that it is one of the *Trikâya* (three bodies), with the “power of assuming any form of appearance in order to propagate Buddhism” (Eitel’s idea); again, that “it is the incarnate *avatâra* of a deity” (*ibid.*), and so on. Occultism, on the other hand, says that Nirmânakâya, although literally meaning a transformed “body,” is actually a state. The form is that of the adept or yogi who enters or chooses that *post mortem* condition in preference to the Dharmakâya or absolute Nirvânic state. He does this because the latter *kâya* separates him forever from the world of form, conferring upon him a state of selfish bliss in which no other living being can participate; the adept is thus precluded from the possibility of helping humanity, or even *devas*. As a Nirmânakâya, however, the man leaves behind him only his physical body and retains every other “principle” except the Kamic—for he has crushed this out forever from his nature during life, and it can never be resurrected in his *post mortem* state. Thus, instead of entering into selfish bliss, he chooses a life of self-sacrifice—an existence that ends only with the life-cycle—in order to be enabled to help mankind in an invisible yet most effective manner. (See *The Voice of the Silence*, third treatise, “The Seven Portals”.) Thus a Nirmânakâya is not, as popularly believed, the body “in which a Buddha or a Bodhisattva appears on earth,” but truly one who, whether a *Chutuktu* or a *Khubilkhan*, an

adept or a yogi during life, has since become a member of that invisible Host which always protects and watches over Humanity within Karmic limits. Often mistaken for a “Spirit”, a *Deva*, God himself, etc., **Nirmânakâya** is always a protecting, compassionate, truly a guardian angel to him who becomes worthy of his help. Whatever objection may be brought forward against this doctrine; however much it is denied because, indeed, it has never been made public in Europe until now and therefore, since it is unknown to Orientalists, it must necessarily be “a myth of modern invention”—no one will be bold enough to say that this idea of helping suffering mankind at the price of one’s own almost interminable self-sacrifice is not one of the grandest and noblest that was ever evolved from the human brain.

**Nirmathya** (*Sk*.). The sacred fire produced by the friction of two pieces of wood—the “fire” called *Pavâmâna* in the *Purânas*. The allegory contained within it is an occult teaching.

**Nirriti** (*Sk*.). A goddess of Death and Decay.

**Nirukta** (*Sk*.). An *anga* or limb, a division of the *Vedas*; a glossarial comment.

**Nirupadhi** (*Sk*.). Attributeless; the negation of attributes.

**Nirvâna** (*Sk*.). According to the Orientalists, the entire “blowing out”, like the flame of a candle, the utter extinction of existence. But in the esoteric explanations, it is the state of absolute existence and absolute consciousness into which the Ego of a man who has reached the highest degree of perfection and holiness during life goes after the body dies, and occasionally, as in the case of Gautama Buddha and others, during life. (See “*Nirvânî*”.)

**Nirvânî** (*Sk*.). One who has attained *Nirvâna*—an emancipated soul. Every scholar who has visited China, India, and Japan is well aware that *Nirvâna* means nothing of the kind asserted by Orientalists. It is “escape from misery”, but only from that of matter; freedom from *Klêsha*, or *Kâma*, and the complete extinction of animal desires. If we are told that *Abidharma* defines *Nirvâna* “as a state of absolute annihilation”, we agree, adding to the last word the qualification “of everything connected with matter or the physical world”, and this is simply because the latter (as well as all in it) is illusion, *mâyâ*. *Sâkyamûnî* Buddha said in the last moments of his life that “the spiritual body is immortal” (*See Sans. Chin. Dict.*). As Mr. *Eitel*, the scholarly Sinologist, explains it: “The popular exoteric systems agree in defining *Nirvâna* *negatively* as a state of absolute exemption from the circle of transmigration; as a state of entire freedom from all forms of existence; to begin with, freedom from all passion and exertion; a state of indifference to all sensibility”—and he might have added “the death of all compassion for the world of suffering”. And this is why the *Bodhisattvas*, who prefer the *Nirmânakâya* to the *Dharmakâya* vesture, stand higher in the popular estimation than the *Nirvânîs*. But the same

The scholar adds that: "Positively (and esoterically) they define Nirvâna as the highest state of spiritual bliss, as absolute immortality through the absorption of the soul (or rather the spirit) into itself, while preserving individuality so that, *for example*, Buddhas, after entering Nirvâna, may reappear on earth"—that is, in the future Manvantara.

**Nishada** (Sanskrit). (1) One of the seven qualities of sound—the single and sole attribute of Akâsa; (2) the *seventh* note of the Hindu musical scale; (3) an outcast offspring of a Brahman father and a Sudra mother; (4) a range of mountains south of Meru and north of the Himalayas.

**Nissi** (Chaldean). One of the seven Chaldean gods.

**Nîti** (Sanskrit). Literally: Prudence, ethics.

**Nitya Parivrita** (Sanskrit). Literally: continuous extinction.

**Nitya Pralaya** (Sanskrit). Literally: "perpetual" Pralaya or dissolution. It refers to the constant and imperceptible changes experienced by the atoms, which last as long as a Mahâmanvantara—a whole age of Brahmâ, which requires fifteen digits to express. It is a stage of chronic change and dissolution, consisting of the stages of growth and decay. It lasts for the duration of "Seven Eternities." (See *Secret Doctrine* I. 371, II. 69, 310.) There are four kinds of Pralayas or states of changelessness: the Naimittika, when Brahmâ sleeps; the Prâkritika, a partial Pralaya of anything during a Manvantara; Atyantika, when man has identified himself with the One Absolute—a synonym of Nirvâna; and Nitya, for physical things especially, as a state of profound and dreamless sleep.

**Nitya Sarga** (Sanskrit). The state of constant creation or evolution, as opposed to *Nitya Pralaya*—the state of perpetual, incessant dissolution (or change of atoms), the disintegration of molecules, and therefore the change of forms.

**Nizir** (Chaldean). The "Deluge Mountain"; the Ararat of the Babylonians, featuring "Xisuthrus" as their Noah.

**Nixies.** The water-sprites or Undines.

**Niyashes** (Mazdean). Parsi prayers.

**Nofir-hotpoo** (Egyptian). The same as the god Khonsoo, the lunar god of Thebes. Literally: "he who is in absolute rest." Nofir-hotpoo is one of the three persons of the Egyptian trinity, composed of Ammon, Mooth, and their son Khonsoo or Nofir-hotpoo.

**Nogah** (Chaldean). Venus, the planet; glittering splendor.

**Noo** (Egyptian). Primordial waters of space called "Father-Mother"; the "face of the deep" in the Bible; for above Noo hovers the Breath of Kneph, who is represented with the Mundane Egg in his mouth.

**Noom** (Egyptian). A celestial sculptor in the Egyptian legends who creates a beautiful girl whom he sends, like another Pandora, to *Batoo* (or "man"), whose happiness is thereafter destroyed. The "sculptor" or artist is the same as Jehovah, the architect of the world, and the girl is "Eve."

**Noon** (Eg.). The celestial river which flows in *Noot*, the cosmic abyss or *Noo*. As all the gods have been generated in the river (the *Gnostic Pleroma*), it is called “the Father-Mother of the gods.”

**Noor Ilahee** (Arab.). “The light of the *Elohim*,” literally. This light is believed by some Muslims to be transmitted to mortals “through a hundred prophet-leaders.” Divine knowledge; the Light of the Secret Wisdom.

**Noot** (Eg.). The heavenly abyss in the *Ritual* or the Book of the Dead. It is infinite space personified in the Vedas by Aditi, the goddess who, like Noon (see above), is the “mother of all the gods.”

**Norns** (Scand.). The three sister goddesses in the Edda, who make known to men the degrees of *Orlog* or Fate. They are shown as coming out of the unknown distances enveloped in a dark veil to the Ash *Yggdrasil* (see entry), and “sprinkle it daily with water from the Fountain of Urd, so that it may not wither but remain green and fresh and strong” (Asgard and the Gods). Their names are “Urd,” the Past; “Werdandi,” the Present; and “Skuld,” the Future, “which is either rich in hope or dark with tears.” Thus they reveal the degrees of Fate “for out of the past and present the events and actions of the future are born” (loc. cit.).

**Notaricon** (Kab.). A division of the practical Kabbalah; it deals with the formation of words from the initials or finals of the words in every sentence; or conversely, it forms a sentence of words whose initials or finals are those of some word. [w.w.w.]

**Noumenon** (Gr.). The true essential nature of being as distinguished from the illusory objects of sense.

**Nous** (Gr.). A Platonic term for the Higher Mind or Soul. It means Spirit as distinct from the animal Soul—*psyche*; divine consciousness or mind in man. *Nous* was the designation given to the Supreme deity (the third *logos*) by Anaxagoras. Taken from Egypt where it was called *Nout*, it was adopted by the Gnostics for their first conscious *Æon* which, for Occultists, is the third *logos*, cosmically, and the third “principle” (from above) or *manas*, in man. (See “Nout”).

**Nout** (Gr.). In the Pantheon of the Egyptians, it meant the “One-only-One,” because they did not proceed in their popular or exoteric religion higher than the *third manifestation* which radiates from the *Unknown and the Unknowable*—the first unmanifested and the second *logoi* in the esoteric philosophy of every nation. The *Nous* of Anaxagoras was the *Mahat* of the Hindu *Brahmâ*, the *first manifested Deity*—“the Mind or Spirit self-potent”; this creative Principle being, of course, the *primum mobile* of everything in the Universe—its Soul and Ideation. (See “Seven Principles” in man).

**Number Nip**. An Elf, the mighty King of the Riesengebirge, the most powerful of the genii in Scandinavian and German folklore.

**Nuns**. There were nuns in ancient Egypt as well as in Peru and old

**O.**—The fifteenth letter and fourth vowel in the English alphabet. It has no equivalent in Hebrew, as that alphabet is entirely made up of consonants, with only one exception. As a numeral, the ancients used it to represent 11; when written with a dash above it (Ō), it signified 11,000. It was considered a very sacred letter by other ancient peoples as well. In **Devanagari** <note>original: "Dêvanâgarî"; the script used for Sanskrit, meaning "the script of the city of the gods"</note>, its significance varies, but there is not enough space here to provide specific examples.

**Oak**, sacred. The oak was a most holy tree to the Druids, as it was to the ancient Greeks. This is supported by the writings of Pherecydes in his *cosmogony* <note>an account of the origin of the universe</note>, who speaks of the sacred oak "in whose lush branches a serpent (symbolizing wisdom) dwells and cannot be driven out." Every nation had its own sacred trees, most notably the Hindus.

**Oannes** (*Greek*). Musarus Oannes, the Annedotus <note>from the Greek *Annedotos*, a title given to these teachers</note>, is known in the Chaldean "legends" passed down by Berosus and other ancient writers as **Dag** or **Dagon**, the "man-fish." Oannes appeared to the early Babylonians as a reformer and an instructor. Emerging from the Erythraean Sea <note>The ancient name for the body of water including the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf</note>, he brought civilization, literacy, sciences, law, astronomy, and religion to the people. He also taught them agriculture, geometry, and the arts in general. 

There were other "Annedoti" who followed him, five in total—representing our current human race, which is the *fifth*—who were "all like Oannes in form and taught the same things." However, Musarus Oannes was the first to appear. This occurred during the reign of Ammenon, the third of the ten kings who lived before the Great Flood; this dynasty ended with Xisuthrus, the Chaldean version of Noah (See "**Xisuthrus**"). 

Oannes was described as "a rational animal... whose body was that of a fish, but who had a *human head* underneath the fish's head. He also had *feet* below, similar to those of a man, attached to the fish's tail, and his voice and language were human and articulate" (according to the historians Polyhistor and Apollodorus). 

This description provides the key to the allegory. It identifies Oannes as a man, a "priest," and an *Initiate*. The archaeologist Austen Henry Layard showed long ago (See his work *Nineveh*) that the "fish's head" was simply a headpiece—a **mitre** worn by priests and gods, shaped like a fish's head. This same shape, only slightly modified, can still be seen today on the heads of high-ranking Lamas and Roman Catholic Bishops. Osiris also wore such a mitre. The fish's tail is simply the train of a long, stiff cloak, as shown on some Assyrian tablets. This form is even preserved in the *sacerdotal* <note>priestly</note> gold-cloth garments worn during services by modern Greek Orthodox priests. 

This allegory of Oannes, the Annedotus, reminds us of the "Dragons" and "Snake-Kings"—the **Nagas** of Buddhist legend who teach wisdom to people by lakes and rivers and eventually become converts to the "Good Law" and become **Arhats** <note>enlightened beings</note>. The meaning is clear: the "fish" is an ancient...

Thus, one sees why Occultism places <term>Oannes</term> and the other <term>Annedoti</term> in the group of those ancient "adepts" who were called "marine" or "water dragons"—*<term>Nâgas</term>*. Water represented their human origin (as it is a symbol of earth and matter and also of purification), in contrast to the "fire Nâgas" or the immaterial, Spiritual Beings, whether celestial <term>Bodhisattvas</term> or Planetary <term>Dhyânis</term>, who were also regarded as the instructors of mankind. The hidden meaning becomes clear to the <term>Occultist</term> once he is told that "this being (<term>Oannes</term>) was accustomed to pass the day among men, teaching; and when the Sun had set, he retired again into the sea, passing the night in the deep, 'for he was *amphibious*,'" meaning he belonged to two planes: the spiritual and the physical. For the Greek word *amphibios* means simply "life on two planes," from *amphi*, "on both sides," and *bios*, "life." The word was often applied in antiquity to those men who, though still wearing a human form, had made themselves almost divine through knowledge, and lived as much in the spiritual supersensory regions as on earth. <term>Oannes</term> is dimly reflected in Jonah, and even in John the Precursor <note>John the Baptist</note>, both of whom are connected with Fish and Water.

**Ob** (*Heb.*). The astral light—or rather, its harmful evil currents—was personified by the Jews as a Spirit, the Spirit of *Ob*. Among them, anyone who dealt with spirits and <term>necromancy</term> was said to be possessed by the Spirit of *Ob*.

**Obeah.** Sorcerers and sorceresses of Africa and the West Indies. A sect of black magicians, snake-charmers, enchanters, etc.

**Occult Sciences.** The science of the secrets of nature—physical and psychic, mental and spiritual; called <term>Hermetic</term> and <term>Esoteric</term> Sciences. In the West, the <term>Kabbalah</term> may be named; in the East, mysticism, magic, and <term>Yoga</term> philosophy, which latter is often referred to by the <term>Chelas</term> <note>disciples</note> in India as the *seventh* "<term>Darshana</term>" (school of philosophy), as there are only six Darshanas in India known to the world of the uninitiated. These sciences are, and have been for ages, hidden from the common people for the very good reason that they would never be appreciated by the selfish educated classes, nor understood by the uneducated; while the former might misuse them for their own profit, and thus turn the divine science into *black magic*. It is often raised as an accusation against the <term>Esoteric</term> philosophy and the <term>Kabbalah</term> that their literature is full of "a barbarous and meaningless jargon" unintelligible to the ordinary mind. <header>THEOSOPHICAL</header>

**Ogdoad** (*Gr.*). The tetrad or "quaternary" reflecting itself produced the ogdoad, the "eight," according to the Marcosian Gnostics. The eight great gods were called the "sacred Ogdoad."

**Ogham** (*Celtic*). A mystery language belonging to the early Celtic races and used by the Druids. One form of this language consisted of associating the leaves of certain trees with letters; this was called *Beth-luis-nion Ogham*. To form words and sentences, the leaves were strung on a cord in the proper order. Godfrey Higgins suggests that to complete the mystification, certain other leaves which meant nothing were interspersed. [w.w.w.]

**Ogîr** or *Hlêr* (*Scand.*). A chief of the giants in the *Edda* and the ally of the gods. He is the highest of the water-gods and the same as the Greek Okeanos.

**Ogmius**. The god of wisdom and eloquence of the Druids; hence, he is Hermes in a sense.

**Ogygia** (*Gr.*). An ancient submerged island known as the Isle of Calypso, identified by some with Atlantis. This is correct in a certain sense. But then, which portion of Atlantis was it, since the latter was a continent rather than just an "enormous" island!

**Oïtzoe** (*Pers.*). The invisible goddess whose voice spoke through the rocks. According to Pliny, the *Magi* were required to consult her for the election of their kings.

**Okhal** (*Arab.*). The "High" priest of the Druzes, an initiator into their mysteries.

**Okhema** (*Gr.*). A Platonic term meaning "vehicle" or body.

**Okuthor** (*Scand.*). The same as Thor, the "thunder god."

**Olympus** (*Gr.*). A mountain in Greece, the abode of the gods according to Homer and Hesiod.

**Om** or *Aum* (*Sk.*). A mystic syllable, the most solemn of all words in India. It is "an invocation, a benediction, an affirmation, and a promise"; and it is so sacred that it is indeed the *word spoken at low breath in occult, primitive masonry*. No one must be nearby when the syllable is pronounced for a specific purpose. This word is usually placed at the beginning of sacred scriptures and is prefixed to prayers. It is a compound of three letters, *a, u, and m*, which in popular belief are typical of the three Vedas and also of the three gods—**A** (Agni), **V** (Varuna), and **M** (Maruts), or Fire, Water, and Air. In esoteric philosophy, these are the three sacred fires, or the "triple fire" in the Universe and Man, among many other things. Occultly, this "triple fire" also represents the highest *Tetraktys*, as it is typified by the Agni named *Abhimânin* and his transformation into his three sons: *Pâvana*, *Pavmâna*, and *Suchi*, "who drinks up water"—that is, he who destroys material desires. This monosyllable is called *Udgitha* and is sacred to both Brahmins and Buddhists.

**Omito-Fo** (*Chin.*). The name of Amita-Buddha in China.

**Omkâra** (*Sk.*). The same as Aum or Om. It is also the name of one of the twelve lingams that was represented by a secret and most sacred shrine at Ujjain—no longer existing since the time of Buddhism.

**Omoroka** (*Chald.*). The “sea” and the woman who personifies it according to Berosus, or rather Apollodorus. As the *divine water*, however, Omoroka is the reflection of Wisdom from on high.

**Onech** (*Heb.*). The Phoenix, so named after Enoch or Phenoch. For Enoch (also Khenoch) means literally the *initiator* and *instructor*, hence the Hierophant who reveals the *last mystery*. The Phoenix bird is always associated with a tree, the mystical *Ababel* of the Koran, the *Tree of Initiation* or of knowledge.

**Onofre** or **Oun-nofre** (*Eg.*). The King of the land of the Dead, the Underworld, and in this capacity the same as Osiris, “who resides in Amenti at Oun-nefer, king of eternity, great god manifested in the celestial abyss.” (A hymn of the XIXth dynasty). (See also “Osiris”).

**Ophanim** (*Heb.*). More correctly written Auphanim. The “wheels” seen by Ezekiel and by John in the Revelation—world-spheres (*Secret Doctrine* I., 92). The symbol of the Cherubs or Karoubs (the Assyrian Sphinxes). As these beings are represented in the Zodiac by Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius, or the Bull, the Lion, the Eagle and Man, the occult meaning of these creatures being placed in company of the four Evangelists becomes evident. In the *Kabbalah* they are a group of beings allotted to the Sephira Chakmah, Wisdom.

**Ophis** (*Gr.*). The same as Chnuphis or *Kneph*, the *Logos*; the good serpent or Agathodaemon.

**Ophiomorphos** (*Gr.*). The same, but in its material aspect, as the Ophis-Christos. With the Gnostics the Serpent represented “Wisdom in Eternity.”

**Ophis-Christos** (*Gr.*). The serpent Christ of the Gnostics.

**Ophiozenes** (*Gr.*). The name of the Cypriote charmers of venomous serpents and other reptiles and animals.

**Ophites** (*Gr.*). A Gnostic Fraternity in Egypt, and one of the earliest sects of Gnosticism, or *Gnosis* (Wisdom, Knowledge), known as the “Brotherhood of the Serpent.” It flourished early in the second century, and while holding some of the principles of Valentinus, it had its own occult rites and symbology. A living serpent, representing the *Christos*-principle (*i.e.*, the divine reincarnating Monad, not Jesus the man), was displayed in their mysteries and reverenced as a symbol of wisdom, Sophia, the type of the all-good and all-wise. The Gnostics were not a Christian sect, in the common acceptance of this term, as the *Christos* of pre-Christian thought and the Gnosis was not the “god-man” Christ, but the divine Ego, made one with Buddhi. Their *Christos* was the “Eternal Initiate,” the Pilgrim, typified by hundreds of serpent symbols for several thousands of years before the “Christian” era, so—

One can see it on the “Belzoni tomb” from Egypt, as a winged serpent with three heads (<term>Atma-Buddhi-Manas</term>), and four human legs, symbolizing its androgynous character; on the walls of the descent to the sepulchral chambers of Rameses V., it is found as a snake with vulture’s wings, the vulture and hawk being solar symbols. “The heavens are scribbled over with endless snakes” writes Herschel regarding the Egyptian chart of stars. “The *Meissi* (Messiah?) meaning the *Sacred Word*, was a good serpent”, writes Bonwick in his *Egyptian Belief*. “This serpent of goodness, with its head crowned, was mounted upon a cross and formed a sacred standard of Egypt”. The Jews borrowed it in their “brazen serpent of Moses”. Tertullian, whether knowingly or unknowingly, mixed up the two. The four-winged serpent is the god <term>Cnuphis</term>. The good serpent bore the cross of life around its neck, or suspended from its mouth. The winged serpents become the *Seraphim* (*Seraph*, *Saraph*) of the Jews. In the 87th chapter of the *Ritual* (the <term>Book of the Dead</term>) the human soul transformed into <term>Bata</term>, the omniscient serpent, says—“I am the serpent Ba-ta, of many years, Soul of the Soul, laid out and born daily; I am the Soul that descends on the earth”, *i.e.*, the <term>Ego</term>.

**<term>Orai</term> (Gr.).** The name of the angel-ruler of Venus, according to the Egyptian Gnostics.

**<term>Orcus</term> (Gr.).** The bottomless pit in the *Codex* of the Nazarenes.

**<term>Örgelmir</term> (Scand.).** Literally, “seething clay”. The same as <term>Ymir</term>, the giant; the unruly, turbulent, erratic being who is the type of primordial matter. Out of his body, after killing him, the sons of Bör created a new earth. He is also the cause of the <term>Deluge</term> in the Scandinavian Lays, for he flung his body into <term>Ginnungagap</term>, the yawning abyss; when the latter was filled with it, the blood flowed over and produced a great flood in which all the <term>Hrimthurses</term>, the frost giants, were drowned; only one of them, the cunning <term>Bergelmir</term>, saves himself and his wife in a boat and became the father of a new race of giants. “And there were giants on the earth in those days”.

**<term>Orion</term> (Gr.).** The same as <term>Atlas</term>, who supports the world on his shoulders.

**<term>Orlog</term> (Scand.).** Fate, destiny, whose agents were the three <term>Norns</term>, the Norse *Parcæ*.

**<term>Ormazd</term> or <term>Ahura Mazda</term> (Zend).** The god of the Zoroastrians or the modern Parsis. He is symbolized by the sun, as being the Light of Lights. Esoterically, he is the synthesis of his six *Amshaspends* or <term>Elohim</term>, and the creative *Logos*. In the Mazdean exoteric system, <term>Ahura Mazda</term> is the supreme god, and one with the supreme god of the Vedic age—<term>Varuna</term>, if we read the *Vedas* literally.

The four chief aspects of <term>Osiris</term> were—<term>Osiris Phtah</term> (Light), the spiritual aspect; <term>Osiris-Horus</term> (Mind), the intellectual aspect; <term>Osiris-Lunus</term>, the “Lunar” or psychic, astral aspect; and <term>Osiris-Typhon</term>, the demonic, or physical, material, and therefore passionate, turbulent aspect. In these four aspects, he symbolizes the dual <term>Ego</term>—the divine and the human, the cosmic-spiritual and the terrestrial.

Of the many supreme gods, this Egyptian conception is the most suggestive and the grandest, as it embraces the whole range of physical and metaphysical thought. As a solar deity, he had twelve minor gods under him—the twelve signs of the <term>Zodiac</term>. Though his name is the “*Ineffable*,” his forty-two attributes each bore one of his names, and his seven dual aspects completed the forty-nine, or 7×7; the former were symbolized by the fourteen members of his body, or twice seven. As such, he is born into the world. He came as a benefactor to relieve man of trouble . . . . . In his efforts to do good, he encounters evil . . . . . and he is temporarily overcome. He is killed . . . . *Osiris* is buried. His tomb was the object of pilgrimage for thousands of years. But he did not rest in his grave. At the end of three days, or forty, he rose again and ascended to Heaven. This is the story of his *Humanity*” (*Egypt. Belief*). **Ossa.** *(Gr.).* A mountain, the tomb of the giants (allegorically).

**Otz-Chiim.** *(Heb.).* The Tree of Life, or rather of Lives; a name given to the <term>Ten Sephiroth</term> when arranged in a diagram of three columns. <note>W.W.W.</note>

**Oulam,** or *Oulom (Heb.).* This word does not mean "eternity" or infinite duration, as translated in the texts, but simply an extended period of time, for which neither the beginning nor the end can be known.

**Ouranos** *(Gr.).* The whole expanse of Heaven called the "Waters of Space," the Celestial Ocean, etc. The name very likely comes from the Vedic <term>Varuna</term>, personified as the water god and regarded as the chief <term>Aditya</term> among the seven planetary deities. In Hesiod's *Theogony*, Ouranos (or Uranus) is the same as *Cœlus* (Heavenly), the oldest of all the gods and the father of the divine <term>Titans</term>.

## P.

**P.** — The 16th letter in both the <term>Greek</term> and the <term>English</term> alphabets, and the 17th in the <term>Hebrew</term>, where it is called *<term>pe</term>* or *<term>peh</term>*, and is symbolized by the mouth, corresponding also, as in the <term>Greek</term> alphabet, to the number 80. The <term>Pythagoreans</term> also made it equivalent to 100, and with a dash—thus (<term>P̄</term>), it stood for 400,000. The <term>Kabbalists</term> associated the sacred name of <term>Phodeh</term> (<term>Redeemer</term>) with it, though no valid reason is given for this.

**P and Cross**, generally called the <term>Labarum</term> of <term>Constantine</term>. It was, however, one of the oldest emblems in <term>Etruria</term> before the <term>Roman Empire</term>. It was also the sign of <term>Osiris</term>. Both the long <term>Latin</term> and the <term>Greek pectoral</term> crosses are <term>Egyptian</term>, the former being very often seen in the hand of <term>Horus</term>. “The <term>cross</term> and <term>Calvary</term>, so common in <term>Europe</term>, occur on the breasts of <term>mummies</term>” (<term>Bonwick</term>).

**Pachacamac** (*<term>Peruv</term>*.). The name given by the <term>Peruvians</term> to the <term>Creator</term> of the <term>universe</term>, represented as a *<term>host of creators</term>*. On his altar, only the first-fruits and flowers were laid by the pious.

**Pacis Bull**. The divine <term>Bull of Hermonthes</term>, sacred to <term>Amoun-Horus</term>; the <term>Bull Netos</term> of <term>Heliopolis</term> was sacred to <term>Amoun-Ra</term>.

**Padârthas** (*<term>Sk</term>*.). <term>Predicates</term> of existing things; so named in the <term>Vaises-hika</term> or “<term>atomic</term>” system of philosophy founded by <term>Kanâda</term>. This school is one of the six <term>Darshanas</term>.

**Padmâ** (*<term>Sk</term>*.). The <term>Lotus</term>; a name for <term>Lakshmi</term>, the <term>Hindu Venus</term>, who is the *<term>wife</term>*, or the <term>female aspect</term>, of <term>Vishnu</term>.

**Padma Âsana** (*<term>Sk</term>*.). A <term>posture</term> prescribed to and practiced by some <term>Yogis</term> for developing <term>concentration</term>.

**Padma Kalpa** (*<term>Sk</term>*.). The name of the last <term>Kalpa</term> or the preceding <term>Manvantara</term>, which was a year of <term>Brahmâ</term>.

**Padma Yoni** (*<term>Sk</term>*.). A <term>title of Brahmâ</term> (also called <term>Abjayoni</term>), meaning the “<term>lotus-born</term>.”

**Pæan** (*<term>Gr</term>*.). A <term>hymn of rejoicing and praise</term> in honor of the <term>sun-god Apollo</term> or <term>Helios</term>.

**Pagan** (*<term>Lat</term>*.). Originally meaning nothing worse than a <term>dweller in the country</term> or the <term>woods</term>; one far removed from the <term>city-temples</term>, and therefore unacquainted with the <term>state religion</term> and <term>ceremonies</term>. The word “<term>heathen</term>” has a similar significance, meaning one who lives on the <term>heaths</term> and in the <term>country</term>. Now, however, both have come to mean <term>idolaters</term>.

**Pagan Gods**. This term is mistakenly understood to mean <term>idols</term>.

With this exception, and especially whenever represented by an idol or in anthropomorphic form, the gods represent symbolically—in the <term>Hindu</term>, <term>Egyptian</term>, or <term>Chaldean</term> <term>Pantheons</term>—formless spiritual <term>Potencies</term> of the “Unseen <term>Cosmos</term>.”

His name means ALL. He was the inventor of the <term>Pandean pipes</term>; and no nymph who heard their sound could resist the fascination of the great <term>Pan</term>, despite his grotesque figure. <term>Pan</term> is related to the <term>Mendesian goat</term> only insofar as the latter represents, as a talisman of great occult potency, nature’s creative force. The whole of the <term>Hermetic philosophy</term> is based on nature’s hidden secrets, and just as <term>Baphomet</term> was undeniably a <term>Kabbalistic talisman</term>, so the name of <term>Pan</term> was of great magical efficiency in what <term>Eliphas Levi</term> would call the “<term>Conjuration of the Elementals</term>.” There is a well-known religious legend which has been current in the Christian world since the time of <term>Tiberius</term>, to the effect that “great <term>Pan</term> is dead.” But people are greatly mistaken in this; neither nature nor any of her forces can ever die. A few of these may be left unused, and being forgotten, lie dormant for many centuries. But as soon as the proper conditions are provided, they awaken to act again with tenfold power.

**Panaenus** (*<term>Gr</term>.*). A <term>Platonic</term> philosopher in the <term>Alexandrian school</term> of <term>Philaletheans</term>.

**Pancha Krishtaya** (*Sk*.). The five races.

**Panchakâma** (*Sk*.). Five methods of sensuousness and sensuality.

**Panchakritam** (*Sk*.). An element combined with small portions of the other four elements.

**Panchama** (*Sk*.). One of the five qualities of musical sound—the fifth—with Nishâda and Daivata completing the seven; it corresponds to G of the diatonic scale.

**Panchânana** (*Sk*.). “Five-faced,” a title of Siva; an allusion to the five races (since the beginning of the first) which he represents as the ever-reincarnating Kumâra throughout the Manvantara. In the sixth root-race, he will be called the “six-faced.”

**Panchâsikha** (*Sk*.). One of the seven Kumâras who went to pay worship to Vishnu on the island of Swetadwipa in the allegory.

**Panchen Rimboche** (*Tib*.). Literally, “the great Ocean, or Teacher of Wisdom.” The title of the Teshu Lama at Tchigadze; an incarnation of Amitabha, the celestial “father” of Chenresi, which is to say that he is an *Avatara* of Tson-kha-pa (See “Sonkhapa”). *De jure*, the Teshu Lama is second after the Delaï Lama; *de facto*, he is higher, since it was Dharma Richen, the successor of Tson-kha-pa at the golden monastery founded by that Reformer and established by the Gelukpa sect (yellow caps), who created the Delaï Lamas at Llhassa and was the first of the dynasty of the “Panchen Rimboche.” While the former (Delaï Lamas) are addressed as “Jewel of Majesty,” the latter enjoy a far higher title, namely “Jewel of Wisdom,” as they are high Initiates.

**Pândavârani** (*Sk*.). Literally, the “Pandava Queen”; Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas. (All these are highly important personified symbols in esoteric philosophy).

**Pândavas** (*Sk*.). The descendants of Pandu.

**Pandora** (*Gr*.). A beautiful woman created by the gods under the orders of Zeus to be sent to Epimetheus, brother of Prometheus; she had charge of a casket in which all the evils, passions, and plagues which torment humanity were locked up. Led by curiosity, Pandora opened this casket and thus set free all the ills which prey on mankind.

**Pandu** (*Sk*.). Literally, “The Pale”; the father of the Pandava Princes, the foes of the *Kurava* in the *Mahâbhârata*.

**Pânini** (*Sk*.). A celebrated grammarian, author of the famous work called *Pâniniyama*; a Rishi, supposed to have received his work from the god Siva. Being ignorant of the epoch in which he lived, Orientalists place his date between 600 B.C. and 300 A.D.

**Pantacle** (*Gr*.). The same as *Pentalpha*; the triple triangle of Pythagoras or the five-pointed star. It was given the name because it

...reproduces the letter **A** (alpha) on its five sides or in five different positions—moreover, its number is composed of the first odd (3) and the first even (2) numbers. It is very occult. In Occultism and the Kabbalah, it stands for *man* or the Microcosm, the “Heavenly Man,” and as such, it was a powerful talisman for keeping evil spirits or Elementals at bay. In Christian theology, it refers to the five wounds of Christ; however, its interpreters fail to add that these “five wounds” were themselves symbolic of the Microcosm, or the “Little Universe,” or again, Humanity. **Pantheist.** One who identifies God with Nature and *vice versa*. Pantheism is often criticized and regarded as reprehensible. But how can a philosopher consider Deity to be infinite, omnipresent, and eternal unless Nature is an aspect of IT, and IT pervades every atom in Nature?

**Panther** (*Hebrew*). According to the *Sepher Toldosh Yeshu*, one of the so-called Apocryphal Jewish Gospels, Jesus was the son of Joseph Panther and Mary, hence Ben Panther. Tradition identifies Panther as a Roman soldier. <note>W.W.W.</note>

**Pâpa-purusha** (*Sanskrit*). Literally, “Man of Sin”: the personification in a human form of every wickedness and sin. Esoterically, it refers to one who is reborn or reincarnated from the state of *Avitchi*—hence, “Soulless.”

**Para** (*Sanskrit*). “Infinite” and “supreme” in philosophy—the final limit. *Param* is the end and goal of existence; *Pâra* is the boundary of boundaries.

**Parabrahm** (*Sanskrit*). Literally, “Beyond Brahmâ.” The Supreme Infinite Brahma, the “Absolute”—the attributeless, secondless reality. The impersonal and nameless universal Principle.

**Paracelsus.** The symbolic name adopted by the greatest Occultist of the Middle Ages—Philip Bombastes Aureolus Theophrastus von Hohenheim—born in the canton of Zurich in 1493. He was the most brilliant physician of his age and the most renowned for curing almost any illness by the power of talismans he prepared himself. He never had a friend but was surrounded by enemies, the most bitter of whom were the clergy and their party. That he was accused of being in league with the devil is logical, nor is it surprising that he was finally murdered by an unknown enemy at the early age of forty-eight. He died at Salzburg, leaving a number of works behind him which are highly valued by Kabbalists and Occultists to this day. Many of his statements have proven prophetic. He was a clairvoyant of great power and one of the most learned and erudite philosophers and

**Paradha** (*Sk.*). The period of one-half the Age of Brahmâ.

**Parama** (*Sk.*). The “one Supreme.”

**Paramapadâtīnava** (*Sk.*). Beyond the condition of Spirit, “more supreme” than Spirit, bordering on the Absolute.

**Paramapadha** (*Sk.*). The place where—according to Visishtadwaïta Vedântins—bliss is enjoyed by those who reach *Moksha* (Bliss). This “place” is not material but made, says the Catechism of that sect, “of *Suddhasatwa*, the essence of which the body of Iswara,” the lord, “is made.”

**Paramapaha** (*Sk.*). A state which is already a conditional existence.

**Paramartha** (*Sk.*). Absolute existence.

**Pâramârthika** (*Sk.*). The one true state of existence according to Vedânta.

**Paramarshis** (*Sk.*). Composed of two words: *parama*, “supreme,” and *Rishis*, or supreme Rishis—Saints.

**Paramâtman** (*Sk.*). The Supreme Soul of the Universe.

**Paranellatons**. In ancient astronomy, the name was applied to certain stars and constellations which are extra-zodiacal, lying above and below the constellations of the Zodiac; they were 36 in number: allotted to the Decans, or one-third parts of each sign. The paranellatons ascend or descend with the Decans alternately; thus, when Scorpio rises, Orion—as its paranellaton—sets, as does Auriga. This gave rise to the fable that the horses of Phaeton (the Sun) were frightened by a Scorpion, and the Charioteer fell into the River Po; that is the constellation of Eridanus, which lies below the star Auriga. <note>W.W.W.</note>

**Paranirvāna** (*Sk.*). Absolute *Non-Being*, which is equivalent to absolute *Being* or “Be-ness,” the state reached by the human Monad at the end of the great cycle (*See Secret Doctrine* I. 135). The same as *Paranishpanna*.

**Parasakṭi** (*Sk.*). “The great Force”—one of the six forces of nature; specifically, that of light and heat.

**Parāsara** (*Sk.*). A Vedic Rishi, the narrator of the *Vishnu Purâna*.

**Paratantra** (*Sk.*). That which has no existence of, or by itself, but only through a dependent or causal connection.

**Paroksha** (*Sk.*). Intellectual apprehension of a truth.

**Parsees**. Also written as Parsis. The followers of Zoroaster. This is the name given to the remnant of the once-powerful Iranian nation which remained true to the religion of its forefathers—fire-worship. This remnant now lives in India, about 50,000 strong, mostly in Bombay and Gujarat.

<header>GLOSSARY</header>

**Pâsa** (*Sk.*). The crucifixion noose of Siva; it is the noose held in his right hand in some of his representations.

**Paschalis,** *Martinez*. A very learned man, a mystic, and an occultist. Born about 1700 in Portugal, he traveled extensively, acquiring knowledge wherever he could in the East—in Turkey, Palestine, Arabia, and Central Asia. He was a great Kabbalist and was the teacher of the person who initiated the Marquis de St. Martin, who founded the mystical Martinist School and Lodges. Paschalis is reported to have died in St. Domingo about 1779, leaving several excellent works behind him.

**Pasht** (*Eg.*). The cat-headed goddess of the Moon, also called *Sekhet*. Her statues and representations are seen in great numbers at the British Museum. She is the wife or female aspect of Ptah (the son of Kneph), the creative principle, or the Egyptian Demiurgus. She is also called *Beset* or *Bubastis*; in these forms, she is both the reuniting and the separating principle. Her motto is "punish the guilty and remove defilement," and one of her emblems is the cat. According to Viscount Rougé, her worship is extremely ancient (3000 B.C.), and she is the mother of the Asiatic race—the race that settled in Northern Egypt. In this capacity, she is called Ouato.

**Pashut** (*Heb.*). "Literal interpretation." One of the four modes of interpreting the Bible used by the Jews.

**Pashyantî** (*Sk.*). The second of the four degrees (*Parâ*, *Pashyantî*, *Madhyamâ*, and *Vaikharî*) into which sound is divided according to its differentiation.

**Pass not,** *The Ring*. The circle within which all those who still labor under the delusion of separateness are confined.

**Passing of the River** (*Kab.*). This phrase may be encountered in works referring to medieval magic: it is the name given to a cipher alphabet used by Kabbalistic Rabbis at an early date; the river referred to is the Chebar. The name will also be found in Latin authors as *Literæ Transitus*. <note>W.W.W.</note>

**Pastophori** (*Gr.*). A certain class of candidates for initiation; they were those who carried the sacred coffin or funeral couch of the Sun-gods—who were killed and resurrected—such as Osiris, Tammuz (or Adonis), Atys, and others, in public processions and also in the temples. The Christians adopted their coffin from the pagans of antiquity.

**Pâtâla** (*Sk.*). The nether world, the antipodes; hence, in popular superstition, the infernal regions, and philosophically, the two Americas, which are antipodal to India. Also, it refers to the South Pole as standing opposite to Meru, the North Pole.

**Pâtaliputra** (*Sk.*). The ancient capital of Magadha, a kingdom of Eastern India, now identified with Patna.

**Pâtanjala** (*Sk.*). The Yoga philosophy; one of the six *Darshanas* or Schools of India.

<header>THEOSOPHICAL</header>

**Patanjali** (*Sanskrit*). The founder of the Yoga philosophy. Orientalists assign him a date of 200 <term>B.C.</term>, while Occultists place him closer to 700 than 600 <term>B.C.</term> Regardless, he was a contemporary of Pânini.

**Pâvaka** (*Sanskrit*). One of the three personified fires—the eldest sons of Abhimânim or Agni, who had forty-five sons. These, along with the original son of Brahmâ (their father Agni) and his three descendants, make up the mystic 49 fires. Pâvaka is the electric fire.

**Pavamâna** (*Sanskrit*). Another of the three fires (see above)—the fire produced by friction.

**Pavana** (*Sanskrit*). God of the wind; the supposed father of the monkey-god Hanuman (See the “Râmâyana”).

**Peling** (*Tibetan*). The name given to all foreigners in Tibet, especially to Europeans.

**Pentacle** (*Greek*). Any geometric figure, especially the one known as the double equilateral triangle or the six-pointed star (like the theosophical pentacle). It is also called Solomon’s seal and, even earlier, “the sign of Vishnu.” It is used by all mystics, astrologers, and similar practitioners.

**Pentagon** (*Greek*), from *pente* (“five”) and *gonia* (“angle”); in geometry, a plane figure with five angles.

**Per-M-Rhu** (*Egyptian*). This name is the recognized pronunciation of the ancient title for the collection of mystical lectures called *The Book of the Dead* in English. Several nearly complete papyri have been found, and there are countless surviving copies of portions of the work. <note>w.w.w.</note>

**Personality.** In Occultism—which divides a human being into seven principles, considering them under the three aspects of the *divine*, the *thinking* or rational, and the *animal man*—this refers to the lower quaternary or the purely astrophysical being. In contrast, “Individuality” refers to the Higher Triad, viewed as a Unity. Thus, the Personality includes all the characteristics and memories of a single physical life, while the Individuality is the imperishable *Ego* which reincarnates and clothes itself in one personality after another.

**Pesh-Hun** (*Tibetan*). From the Sanskrit *pesuna* (“spy”); a title given to Nârada, the meddlesome and troublesome Rishi.

**Phala** (*Sanskrit*). Retribution; the fruit or result of causes.

**Phâlguna** (*Sanskrit*). A name of Arjuna; also the name of a month.

**Phallic** (*Greek*). Anything belonging to sexual worship, or having an external sexual character, such as the Hindu lingham and yoni—the emblems of the male and female generative power. These symbols do not carry the "unclean" significance attributed to them by the Western mind.

**Phanes** (*Greek*). One of the Orphic triad—*Phanes*, *Chaos*, and *Chronos*.

This was also the trinity of the Western people during the pre-Christian period.

<header>GLOSSARY</header>

**Phenomenon (Gr.).** In reality "an appearance," something previously unseen and puzzling when its cause is unknown. Leaving aside various kinds of phenomena—such as cosmic, electrical, chemical, etc.—and focusing only on the phenomena of spiritism, let it be remembered that theosophically and esoterically every "miracle" (from the biblical to the thaumaturgic) is simply a phenomenon. However, no phenomenon is ever a miracle—that is, something supernatural or outside the laws of nature—as all such things are impossible in nature.

**Philaletheans (Gr.).** Literally, "the lovers of truth"; the name is given to the Alexandrian Neo-Platonists, also called Analogeticists and Theosophists. (See *Key to Theosophy*, p. 1, *et seq.*) The school was founded by Ammonius Saccas early in the third century and lasted until the fifth. The greatest philosophers and sages of the day belonged to it.

**Philalethes, *Eugenius*.** The Rosicrucian name assumed by one Thomas Vaughan, a medieval English occultist and Fire Philosopher. He was a great alchemist. <note>w.w.w.</note>

**Philæ (Gr.).** An island in Upper Egypt where a famous temple of that name was situated; travelers can still see its ruins today.

**Philo Judæus.** A Hellenized Jew of Alexandria and a very famous historian and writer; born about 30 B.C., he died about 45 A.D. He should, therefore, have been well acquainted with the greatest event of the first century of our era and the facts about Jesus—his life and the drama of the Crucifixion. Yet he is absolutely silent on the subject, both in his careful list of the then-existing sects and brotherhoods in Palestine and in his accounts of the Jerusalem of his day. He was a great mystic, and his works abound with metaphysics and noble ideas; in terms of esoteric knowledge, he had no rival among the best writers for several centuries. <note>See under "Philo Judæus" in the Glossary of the Key to Theosophy.</note>

**Philosopher’s Stone.** Also called the "Powder of Projection." It is the *Magnum Opus* of the alchemists, an object to be attained by them at all costs—a substance possessing the power of transmuting base metals into pure gold. Mystically, however, the Philosopher’s Stone symbolizes the transmutation of the lower animal nature of man into the highest and divine nature.

**Philostratus (Gr.).** A biographer of Apollonius of Tyana who described the life, travels, and adventures of this sage and philosopher.

**Phla (Gr.).** A small island in Lake Tritonia during the days of Herodotus.

**Phlegiæ (Gr.).** An ancient island submerged in prehistoric days and identified by some writers with Atlantis; also a people in Thessaly.

**Pho (Chin.).** The animal soul.

When the ten <term>Sephiroth</term> are arranged in the <term>Tree of Life</term>, two vertical lines separate them into three Pillars: namely, the Pillar of Severity, the Pillar of Mercy, and the central Pillar of Mildness. <term>Binah</term>, <term>Geburah</term>, and <term>Hod</term> form the first (Severity); <term>Kether</term>, <term>Tiphereth</term>, <term>Jesod</term>, and <term>Malkuth</term> form the central pillar; <term>Chokmah</term>, <term>Chesed</term>, and <term>Netzach</term> form the Pillar of Mercy. <note>w.w.w.</note>

**Pillars of Hermes**. Like the “<term>pillars of Seth</term>” (with which *they are identified*), they served to commemorate occult events and various esoteric secrets that were symbolically engraved upon them. This was a universal practice. <term>Enoch</term> is also said to have constructed pillars.

**Pingala** (*Sk.*). The great <term>Vedic</term> authority on the <term>Prosody</term> and <term>chhandas</term> (meters) of the <term>Vedas</term>. He lived several centuries B.C.

**Pippala** (*Sk.*). The <term>tree of knowledge</term>: the mystic fruit of that tree “upon which came <term>Spirits who love Science</term>.” This is allegorical and occult.

<page-num>240</page-num>
<header>THEOSOPHICAL</header>

...thought to become eternal and divine, **<term>Porphyry</term>** devoted his whole time to considering how philosophy applies to practical life. “For him, the goal of philosophy is morality,” says a biographer, “we might almost say, holiness—the healing of human infirmities, the giving to him a purer and more vigorous life. Mere knowledge, however true, is not sufficient in itself; knowledge aims for a *life* in accordance with *<term>Nous</term>*”—which the biographer translates as “reason.” As we interpret *<term>Nous</term>*, however, not as reason, but as mind (<term>Manas</term>) or the divine eternal Ego in man, we would translate the idea esoterically and make it read: “the occult or secret knowledge aims for an earthly life in accordance with *<term>Nous</term>*, or our everlasting reincarnating Ego,” which would be more consistent with Porphyry’s idea, as it is with esoteric philosophy. (See Porphyry’s *De Abstinentia* i., 29.) Of all the <term>Neo-Platonists</term>, Porphyry came closest to real <term>Theosophy</term> as it is now taught by the Eastern secret school. This is shown by all our modern critics and writers on the Alexandrian school, for “he held that the Soul should be freed as much as possible from the bonds of matter, . . . and be ready . . . to cut off the whole body.” (*Ad Marcellam*, 34.) He recommends practicing abstinence, saying that “we would be like the gods if we could abstain from vegetable as well as animal food.” He reluctantly accepts theurgy and mystical incantations, as these are “powerless to purify the noetic (<term>manasic</term>) principle of the soul”: theurgy can “only cleanse the lower or psychic portion, and make it capable of perceiving lower beings, such as spirits, angels, and gods” (*Augustine, De Civitate Dei* x., 9), just as Theosophy teaches. “Do not defile the divine,” he adds, “with the vain imaginations of men; you will not injure that which is forever blessed (<term>Buddhi-Manas</term>), but you will blind yourself to the perception of the greatest and most vital truths.” (*Ad Marcellam*, 18.) “If we would be free from the assaults of evil spirits, we must keep ourselves away from those things over which evil spirits have power, for they do not attack the pure soul which has no affinity with them.” (*De Abstinentia* ii., 43.) This is again our teaching. The Church Fathers considered Porphyry their bitterest enemy, the most irreconcilable to Christianity. Finally, and once more as in modern Theosophy, Porphyry—like all the <term>Neo-Platonists</term>, according to St. Augustine—“praised Christ while they disparaged Christianity”; they contended, as we contend, that Jesus “said nothing himself against the pagan deities, but performed wonders with their help.” “They could not call him God as his disciples did, but they honored him as one of the best and wisest of men.” (*De Civitate Dei*, xix., 23.) Yet, “even in the storm of controversy, scarcely a word seems to have been uttered against the personal life of Porphyry. His system prescribed purity and . . . he practiced it.” (See *A Dictionary of Christian Biography*, Vol. IV., “Porphyry”.)

**<term>Poseidonis</term>** (*Greek*). The last remnant of the great Atlantean continent. Plato’s island of **<term>Atlantis</term>** is referred to as an equivalent term in Esoteric Philosophy.

<header>GLOSSARY</header>

**Postel, Guillaume.** A French adept, born in Normandy in 1510. His learning brought him to the attention of Francis I, who sent him to the Levant in search of occult manuscripts, where he was received and initiated by an Eastern Fraternity. On his return to France, he became famous. He was persecuted by the clergy and finally imprisoned by the Inquisition, but he was released from his dungeon by his Eastern brothers. His *Clavis Absconditorum*, a key to things hidden and forgotten, is very celebrated.

**Pot-Amun.** Said to be a Coptic term. The name of an Egyptian priest and hierophant who lived under the earlier Ptolemies. Diogenes Laertius tells us that it signifies one consecrated to the “Amun,” the god of wisdom and secret learning, such as were Hermes, Thoth, and Nebo of the Chaldeans. This must be so, since in Chaldea the priests consecrated to Nebo also bore his name, being called the Neboïm, or in some old Hebrew Kabbalistic works, “Abba Nebu.” The priests generally took the names of their gods. Pot-Amun is credited with having been the first to teach <term>Theosophy</term>, or the outlines of the Secret Wisdom-Religion, to the uninitiated.

**Prabhavâpyaya** *(Sk.)*. That from which all originates and into which all things resolve at the end of the life-cycle.

**Prachetâs** *(Sk.)*. A name of Varuna, the god of water, or esoterically—its principle.

**Prâchetasas** *(Sk.)*. See *Secret Doctrine*, II., 176 and following. Daksha is the son of the Prâchetasas, the ten sons of Prachinavahis. These were men endowed with magic powers in the Purânas who, while practicing religious austerities, remained immersed at the bottom of the sea for 10,000 years. The name is also used for Daksha, called *Prâchetasa*.

**Pradhâna** *(Sk.)*. Undifferentiated substance, called elsewhere and in other schools—Akâsa; and Mulaprakriti or Root of Matter by the Vedantins. In short, it is Primeval Matter.

**Pragna** *(Sk.)* or *Prajna*. A synonym of *Mahat*, the Universal Mind. The capacity for perception. (*S. D.*, I. 139) Consciousness.

**Prahlâda** *(Sk.)*. The son of Tiranyakashipu, the King of the Asuras. As Prahlâda was devoted to Vishnu, of whom his father was the greatest enemy, he became subjected to a variety of tortures and punishments as a result. In order to save his devotee from these, Vishnu assumed the form of Nri-Sinha (man-lion, his fourth avatar) and killed the father.

**Prajâpatis** *(Sk.)*. Progenitors; the givers of life to all on this Earth. They are seven and then ten—corresponding to the seven and ten Kabbalistic Sephiroth; to the Mazdean Amesha-Spentas, etc. Brahmâ, the creator, is called Prajâpati as the synthesis of the Lords of Being.

<term>**Prâkrita**</term> (*Sk.*). One of the provincial dialects of <term>Sanskrit</term>—“the language of the gods,” and therefore, its materialization.
<term>**Prâkritika Pralaya**</term> (*Sk.*). The <term>Pralaya</term> following the Age of <term>Brahmâ</term>, when everything that exists is resolved into its primordial essence (or <term>Prâkriti</term>).
<term>**Prâkriti**</term> (*Sk.*). Nature in general; nature as opposed to <term>Purusha</term>—spiritual nature and <term>Spirit</term>, which together are the “two primeval aspects of the <term>One Unknown Deity</term>.” (*Secret Doctrine*, I. 51.)
<term>**Pralaya**</term> (*Sk.*). A period of obscuration or repose—planetary, cosmic, or universal—the opposite of <term>Manvantara</term> (*S. D.*, I. 370.).
<term>**Pramantha**</term> (*Sk.*). An accessory for producing the sacred fire by friction; specifically, the sticks used by <term>Brahmins</term> to kindle fire by friction.
<term>**Prameyas**</term> (*Sk.*). Things to be proved; the objects of <term>Pramâna</term> or proof.
<term>**Pram-Gimas**</term> (*Lithuanian*). *Literally*, “Master of all,” a title for a deity.
<term>**Pramlochâ**</term> (*Sk.*). A female *Asparas*—a water nymph who beguiled <term>Kandu</term>. (See “*Kandu*.”)
<term>**Prâna**</term> (*Sk.*). <term>Life-Principle</term>; the breath of <term>Life</term>.
<term>**Prânamâya Kosha**</term> (*Sk.*). The vehicle of <term>Prâna</term>, life, or the *Linga Sarira*: a <term>Vedantic</term> term.
<term>**Pranâtman**</term> (*Sk.*). The same as *Sutratmâ*, the eternal germ-thread on which the personal lives of the <term>Ego</term> are strung like beads.
<term>**Pranava**</term> (*Sk.*). A sacred word, equivalent to <term>Aum</term>.
<term>**Prânâyâma**</term> (*Sk.*). The suppression and regulation of the breath in <term>Yoga</term> practice.
<term>**Pranidhâna**</term> (*Sk.*). The fifth observance of the <term>Yogis</term>; ceaseless devotion. (See *Yoga Shâstras*, ii. 32.)
<term>**Prâpti**</term> (*Sk.*). From *Prâp*, to reach. One of the eight <term>Siddhis</term> (powers) of <term>Râj-Yoga</term>. It is the power of transporting oneself from one place to another instantaneously by the mere force of will; it is also the faculty of divination, of healing, and of prophesying—a <term>Yoga</term> power.
<term>**Prasanga Madhyamika**</term> (*Sk.*). A Buddhist school of philosophy in <term>Tibet</term>. Like the <term>Yogâchârya</term> system, it follows the *Mahâyâna* or “<term>Great Vehicle</term>” of precepts; however, having been founded much later than the <term>Yogâchârya</term>, it is not half so rigid and severe. It is a semi-exoteric and very popular system among scholars and laypeople.
<term>**Prashraya**</term>, or *Vinaya* (*Sk.*). “The progenitor of affection.” A title bestowed upon the Vedic <term>Aditi</term>, the “Mother of the Gods.”
<term>**Pratibhâsika**</term> (*Sk.*). The apparent or illusory life.
<term>**Pratisamvid**</term> (*Sk.*). The four “unlimited forms of wisdom” attained by an <term>Arhat</term>; the last of which is the absolute knowledge of and power over the twelve <term>Nidânas</term>. (See “*Nidâna*.”)
