As it grew and developed, the mystic Law of the primitive Kabbalist was transformed and made by the Rabbis to supersede every metaphysical conception with its literal meaning; thus, the Rabbinical and Talmudic Law makes Ain Soph and every divine Principle subservient to itself, and turns its back upon the true esoteric interpretations.

**Thor's Hammer.** A weapon that took the form of the Swastika; called by European Mystics and Masons the "Hermetic Cross," and also the "Jaina Cross," *croix cramponnée*; it is the most archaic, as well as the most sacred and universally respected symbol. (See "Swastika.")

**Thoth (Eg.).** The most mysterious and least understood of gods, whose personal character is entirely distinct from all other ancient deities. While the permutations of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and the rest are so numerous that their individuality is almost lost, Thoth remains changeless from the first to the last Dynasty. He is the god of wisdom and of authority over all other gods. He is the recorder and the judge. His ibis head, and the pen and tablet of the celestial scribe—who records the thoughts, words, and deeds of men and weighs them in the balance—liken him to the type of the esoteric *Lipikas*. His name is one of the first that appears on the oldest monuments. He is the lunar god of the first dynasties, the master of Cynocephalus—the dog-headed ape who stood in Egypt as a living symbol and memorial of the Third Root-Race. (*Secret Doctrine, II. pp. 184 and 185*). He is the "Lord of Hermopolis"—Janus, Hermes, and Mercury combined. He is crowned with an *atef* and the lunar disk, and bears the "Eye of Horus," the *third eye*, in his hand. He is the Greek Hermes, the god of learning, and Hermes Trismegistus, the "Thrice-great Hermes," the patron of physical sciences and the patron and very soul of occult esoteric knowledge. As Mr. J. Bonwick, F.R.G.S., beautifully expresses it:

> "Thoth . . . has a powerful effect on the imagination . . . in this intricate yet beautiful phantasmagoria of thought and moral sentiment of that shadowy past. It is in vain we ask ourselves how man, in the infancy of this human world, in the rudeness of supposed early civilization, could have dreamed of such a heavenly being as Thoth. The lines are so delicately drawn, so intimately and tastefully interwoven, that we seem to be viewing a picture designed by the genius of a Milton and executed with the skill of a Raphael."

Proclus, the disciple of Plotinus, speaking of this mysterious deity, says: "He presides over every kind of condition, leading us to an intelligible essence from this mortal abode, governing the different herds of souls". In other words, Thoth, as the Registrar and Recorder of Osiris in Amenti—the Judgment Hall of the Dead—was a psychopomp deity; while Iamblichus hints that "the cross with a handle (the *thau* or *tau*) which Thoth holds in his hand, was none other than the monogram of his name". Besides the Tau, as the prototype of Mercury, Thoth carries the serpent-rod, an emblem of Wisdom, the rod that becomes the Caduceus. Mr. Bonwick says, "Hermes was the serpent itself in a mystical sense. He glides like that creature, noiselessly, without apparent exertion, along the course of ages. He is . . . . a representative of the spangled heavens. But he is the foe of the bad serpent, for the ibis devoured the snakes of Egypt".

**Thothori Nyan Tsan** (*Tib.*). A King of Tibet in the fourth century. It is narrated that during his reign he was visited by five mysterious strangers, who revealed to him how he might use for his country’s welfare *four precious things* which had fallen from heaven in 331 A.D. in a golden casket, and "the use of which no one knew". These were (1) hands folded as the Buddhist ascetics fold them; (2) a bejeweled *Shorten* (a <term>Stupa</term> built over a receptacle for relics); (3) a gem inscribed with the "Aum mani padme hum"; and (4) the *Zamatog*, a religious work on ethics, which is a part of the <term>Kanjur</term>. A voice from heaven then told the King that after a certain number of generations everyone would learn how precious these four things were. The number of generations stated carried the world to the seventh century, when Buddhism became the accepted religion of Tibet. Making an allowance for legendary license, the four things fallen from heaven, the voice, and the five mysterious strangers may easily be seen to have been historical facts. They were without any doubt five <term>Arhats</term> or <term>Bhikshus</term> from India on their proselytizing tour. Many were the Indian sages who, persecuted in India for their new faith, took themselves to Tibet and China.

**Thrætaona** (*Mazd.*). The Persian Michael, who contended with Zorak or Azhi-Dahaka, the destroying serpent. In the *Avesta*, Azhi-Dahaka is a three-headed monster, one of whose heads is human and the two others are ophidian (serpent-like). Dahaka, who is shown in the Zoroastrian Scriptures as coming from Babylonia, stands as the allegorical symbol of the Assyrian dynasty of King Dahaka (Az-Dahaka) which ruled Asia with an iron hand, and whose banners bore the purple sign of the dragon, *purpureum signum draconis*. Metaphysically, however, the human head denotes the physical man, and the two serpent heads denote the dual manasic principles—the dragon and serpent both standing as symbols of wisdom and occult powers.

**Thread Soul**. The same as *Sutrâtmâ* (see that entry).

<header>GLOSSARY</header>

**Three Degrees** (of Initiation). Every nation had its exoteric and esoteric religion—one for the masses, and the other for the learned and the chosen. For example, the Hindus had three degrees with several sub-degrees. The Egyptians also had three preliminary degrees, personified as the "three guardians of the fire" in the Mysteries. The Chinese had their most ancient *Triad Society*, and the Tibetans still have their "triple step," which was symbolized in the *Vedas* by the three strides of Vishnu. Throughout antiquity, there is an unbounded reverence for the Triad and the Triangle—the first geometrical figure. The ancient Babylonians had three stages of initiation into the priesthood (which was then secret knowledge); the Jews, the Kabbalists, and the mystics borrowed them from the Chaldeans, and the Christian Church borrowed them from the Jews. "There are Two," says Rabbi Simon ben Jochai, "in conjunction with One; hence they are Three, and if they are Three, then they are One."

**Three Faces.** The *Trimûrti* of the Indian Pantheon; the three persons of the one godhead. The *Book of Precepts* says: "There are two Faces, one in *Tushita* (*Devâchân*) and one in *Myalba* (earth); and the Highest Holy unites them and finally absorbs both."

**Three Fires** (*Occult*). The name given to Âtmâ-Buddhi-Manas, which become one when united.

**Thsang Thisrong tsan** (*Tib.*). A king who reigned between the years 728 and 787. He invited Pandit Rakshit from Bengal—who was called Bodhisattva because of his great learning—to settle in Tibet to teach Buddhist philosophy to his priests.

**Thûmi Ṡambhota** (*Sk.*). An Indian mystic and scholar who was the inventor of the Tibetan alphabet.

**Thummim** (*Heb.*). "Perfections." An ornament on the breastplates of the ancient High Priests of Judaism. Modern Rabbis and Hebraists may claim they do not know the joint purposes of the *Thummim* and the *Urim*, but the Kabbalists and Occultists do. They were the instruments of magical divination and oracular communication—both theurgical and astrological. This is shown by the following well-known facts: (1) the name of one of the twelve sons of Jacob was engraved on each of the twelve precious stones, with each of these "sons" representing one of the signs of the zodiac; (2) both were oracular images, like the *teraphim*, and spoke oracles with a voice, and both were agents for hypnosis, placing the priests who wore them into a state of ecstasy. The *Urim* and *Thummim* did not originate with the Hebrews but were borrowed, like most of their other religious rites, from the Egyptians. Among the Egyptians, the mystical scarab, worn on the breast by the high priests, served the same functions. They were thus purely pagan and magical methods of divination; and when the Jewish "Lord God" was called upon to manifest his presence and speak his will through the *Urim* by preliminary incantations, the method of operation was the same as that used by all the non-Jewish priests throughout the world.

**Thumos** (*Gr.*). The astral, animal soul; the *Kâma-Manas*. *Thumos* means passion, desire, and confusion, and is used in this way by Homer. The word is probably derived from the Sanskrit *Tamas*, which has the same meaning.

**Tia-Huanaco** (*Peruv.*). The most magnificent ruins of a prehistoric city in Peru.

**Tiamat** (*Chald.*). A female dragon personifying the ocean; the “great mother” or the living principle of chaos. Tiamat wanted to swallow Bel, but Bel sent a wind which entered her open mouth and killed Tiamat.

**Tiaou** (*Eg.*). A kind of Devachanic state after death.

**Tien-Hoang** (*Chin.*). The twelve hierarchies of Dhyânis.

**Tien-Sin** (*Chin.*). *Literally*, “the heaven of mind”, or the abstract, subjective, ideal heaven. A metaphysical term applied to the Absolute.

**Tikkun** (*Chald.*). Manifested Man or Adam Kadmon, the first ray from the manifested *Logos*.

**Tiphereth** (*Heb.*). Beauty; the sixth of the ten Sephiroth, a masculine active potency corresponding to the Vau (V) of the Tetragrammaton IHVH. It is also called Melekh or King, and the Son. It is the central Sephira of the six that compose Zauir Anpin, the Microprosopus, or Lesser Countenance. It is translated as “Beauty” and “Mildness”.

**Tîrthakas**, or *Tîrthika* and *Tîrthyas* (*Sk.*). “Heretical teachers.” An epithet applied by Buddhist ascetics to the Brahmans and certain Yogis of India.

**Tirthankâra** (*Sk.*). Jaina saints and chiefs, of whom there are twenty-four. It is claimed that one of them was the spiritual Guru of Gautama Buddha. Tirthankâra is a synonym for Jaina.

**Tiryaksrota** (*Sk.*). From *tiryak*, “crooked”, and *srotas*, “(digestive) canal”. The name of the “creation” by Brahmâ of men or beings whose stomachs were in a horizontal position because of their erect position as bipeds. This is a Purânic invention and is absent in Occultism.

**Tishya** (*Sk.*). The same as Kaliyuga, the Fourth Age.

**Titans** (*Gr.*). Giants of divine origin in Greek mythology who made war against the gods. Prometheus was one of them.

**Titikshâ** (*Sk.*). *Literally*, “long-suffering, patience”. Titikshâ, the daughter of Daksha and wife of Dharma (divine law), is its personification.

**To On** (*Gr.*). The “Being”, the “Ineffable All” of Plato. He “whom no one has seen except the Son”.

**Tobo** (*Gnost.*). In the *Codex Nazaræus*, a mysterious being who bears the soul of Adam from Orcus to the place of life, and for that reason is called “the liberator of the soul of Adam”.

**Todas.** A mysterious people of India found in the unexplored remote strongholds of the Nilgiri (Blue) Hills in the Madras Presidency, whose origin, language, and religion are unknown to this day. They are entirely

**Toom** *(Eg.).* A god who emerged from Osiris in his role as the Great Deep, *Noot*. He is the Protean god who generates other gods, "assuming whatever form he likes." He is Fohat. (*Secret Doctrine*, I., 673.)

**Tope.** An artificial mound covering the relics of Buddha or some other great Arhat. These Topes are also called Dagobas.

**Tophet** *(Heb.).* A place in the valley of Gehenna, near Jerusalem, where a constant fire was kept burning, and where children were sacrificed to Baal. The locality is thus the prototype of the Christian Hell, the fiery Gehenna of endless woe.

**Toralva, Dr. Eugene.** A physician who lived in the fourteenth century and who received a demon named Zequiel as a gift from Friar Pietro—a great magician and a Dominican monk—to be his faithful servant. (See *Isis Unveiled* II., 60.)

**Toyâmbudhi** *(Sk.).* A country in the northern part of which lay the "White Island"—*Shveta Dwîpa*—one of the seven Puranic islands or continents.

**Trailokya**, or *Trilokya (Sk.). Literally*, the "three regions" or worlds; the complementary triad to the Brahmanical quaternary of worlds named *Bhuvanatraya*. A lay Buddhist will mention only three divisions of every world, while an uninitiated Brahman will maintain that there are four. The four divisions of the latter are purely physical and sensory, whereas the *Trailokya* of the Buddhist are purely spiritual and ethical. The Brahmanical division may be found fully described under the heading of *Vyahritis*, the difference for now being sufficiently shown in the following comparison:

| Brahmanical Division of the Worlds. | Buddhist Division of the Regions. |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| 1. *Bhur*, earth. | 1. World of Desire, *Kâmadhâtu* or *Kâmalôka*. |
| 2. *Bhuvah*, heaven, firmament. | 2. World of Form, *Rûpadhâtu*. |
| 3. *Swar*, atmosphere, the sky. | |
| 4. *Mahar*, eternal luminous essence. | 3. The formless world, *Arûpadhâtu*. |

All these are the worlds of post-mortem states. For instance, *Kâmalôka* or *Kâmadhâtu*, the region of Mara, is what medieval and modern Kabbalists call the world of astral light and the "world of shells." *Kâmalôka* has, like every other region, its seven divisions, the lowest of which begins on earth or invisibly in its atmosphere; the six others ascend gradually, the highest being the abode of those who have died due to accident, or suicide in a fit of temporary insanity, or who were otherwise victims of external forces. It is a place where all those who have died before the end of the term allotted to them—and whose higher principles do not, therefore, go at once into the Devachanic state—sleep a sweet, dreamless sleep of oblivion. They are either reborn immediately or pass gradually into the Devachanic state. <term>*Rûpadhâtu*</term> is the celestial world of form, or what we call <term>*Devâchân*</term>. Among the uninitiated Brahmans, Chinese, and other Buddhists, the <term>*Rûpadhâtu*</term> is divided into eighteen <term>*Brahmâ*</term> or <term>*Devalokas*</term>. The life of a soul there lasts from half a Yuga up to 16,000 Yugas or Kalpas, and the height of the "Shades" is from half a Yojana up to 16,000 Yojanas (a <term>*Yojana*</term> measuring from five and a half to ten miles!!), and similar theological nonsense evolved from priestly brains. But the Esoteric Philosophy teaches that although for the <term>*Egos*</term> involved for the time being, everything and everyone preserves its form (as in a dream), since <term>*Rûpadhâtu*</term> is a purely mental region and a state, the Egos themselves have no form outside their own consciousness. Esotericism divides this "region" into seven <term>Dhyânas</term>, "regions," or states of contemplation, which are not physical locations but mental representations of them. <term>*Arûpadhâtu*</term>: this "region" is again divided into seven <term>Dhyânas</term>, even more abstract and formless, for this "World" is without any form or desire whatsoever. It is the highest region of the post-mortem <term>Trailokya</term>; and as it is the abode of those who are almost ready for <term>Nirvâna</term>, and is, in fact, the very threshold of the <term>Nirvânic</term> state, it follows that in <term>Arûpadhâtu</term> (or <term>Arûpavachara</term>) there can be neither form nor sensation, nor any feeling connected with our three-dimensional Universe.

**Trees of Life.** From the earliest antiquity, trees were connected with the gods and mystical forces in nature. Every nation had its sacred tree, with unique characteristics and attributes based on natural and occasionally occult properties, as explained in the esoteric teachings. Thus the peepul or <term>*Âshvattha*</term> of India—the abode of <term>Pitris</term> (which are actually elementals) of a lower order—became the <term>Bo-tree</term> or <term>*ficus religiosa*</term> of Buddhists worldwide, since Gautama Buddha reached the highest knowledge and <term>Nirvâna</term> under such a tree. The ash tree, <term>Yggdrasil</term>, is the world-tree of the Norsemen or Scandinavians. The banyan tree is the symbol of spirit and matter: descending to the earth, taking root, and then ascending heavenward again. The triple-leaved <term>*palâsa*</term> is a symbol of the triple essence in the Universe—Spirit, Soul, and Matter. The dark cypress was the world-tree of Mexico and is now the emblem of death, peace, and rest for Christians and Muslims. The fir was held sacred in Egypt, and its cone was carried in religious processions, though it has now almost disappeared from the land of the mummies; the sycamore, the tamarisk, the palm, and the vine were also held sacred. The sycamore was the <term>*Tree of Life*</term> in Egypt and also in Assyria. It was sacred to Hathor at Heliopolis and is now sacred in the same place to the Virgin Mary. Its juice was precious because of its occult powers, just as <term>Soma</term> is with the Brahmans and <term>Haoma</term> with the Parsis. "The fruit and sap of the Tree of Life bestow immortality." A large volume might be written upon these sacred trees of antiquity—the reverence for some of which has survived to this day—without exhausting the subject.

**Tretâ Yuga** (*Sk.*). The second age of the world, a period of 1,296,000 years.

**Triad, or the Three.** The ten <term>Sephiroth</term> are contemplated as a group of three triads: <term>Kether</term>, <term>Chochmah</term>, and <term>Binah</term> form the supernal triad; <term>Chesed</term>, <term>Geburah</term>, and <term>Tiphereth</term>, the second; and <term>Netzach</term>, <term>Hod</term>, and <term>Yesod</term>, the inferior triad. The tenth <term>Sephira</term>, <term>Malkuth</term>, is beyond the three triads. [w.w.w.]

The above is orthodox Western <term>Kabalah</term>. Eastern Occultists recognize but one triad—the upper one (corresponding to <term>Âtmâ-Buddhi</term> and the “Envelope” which reflects their light, the three in one)—and count seven lower <term>Sephiroth</term>, every one of which stands for a “principle”, beginning with the <term>Higher Manas</term> and ending with the <term>Physical Body</term>—of which <term>Malkuth</term> is the representative in the <term>Microcosm</term> and the <term>Earth</term> in the <term>Macrocosm</term>.

**Tri-bhuvana, or Tri-loka** (*Sk.*). The three worlds—<term>Swarga</term>, <term>Bhûmi</term>, <term>Pâtâla</term>—or, Heaven, Earth, and Hell in popular beliefs; esoterically, these are the <term>Spiritual</term> and <term>Psychic</term> (or <term>Astral</term>) regions, and the <term>Terrestrial</term> sphere.

**Tridandî** (*Sk.*). The name generally given to a class or sect of <term>Sanyâsîs</term>, who constantly keep in the hand a kind of club (*danda*) branching off into three rods at the top. The word has various etymologies, and some give the name to the triple Brahmanical thread.

**Tri-dasha** (*Sk.*). Three times ten or “thirty”. This is, in round numbers, the sum of the Indian <term>Pantheon</term>—the thirty-three crores of deities—the twelve <term>Âdityas</term>, the eight <term>Vasus</term>, the eleven <term>Rudras</term>, and the two <term>Ashvins</term>, or thirty-three <term>kotis</term> <note>A koti is ten million</note>, or 330 millions of gods.

**Trigunas** (*Sk.*). The three divisions of the inherent qualities of differentiated matter—that is, of pure stillness (*satva*), of activity and desire (*rajas*), and of stagnation and decay (*tamas*). They correspond with <term>Vishnu</term>, <term>Brahmâ</term>, and <term>Shiva</term>. (See “<term>Trimûrti</term>”.)

**Trijnâna**, (*Sk.*). Literally, “triple knowledge”. This consists of three degrees: (1) belief based on faith; (2) belief based on theoretical knowledge; and (3) belief through personal and practical knowledge.

**Trikâya** (*Sk.*). Literally, three bodies, or forms. This is a most difficult teaching which, however, once understood, explains the mystery of every triad or trinity, and is a true key to every three-fold metaphysical symbol. In its most simple and comprehensive form, it is found in the human Entity in its triple division into spirit, soul, and body, and in the universe, regarded pantheistically, as a unity composed of a Deific, purely spiritual Principle, <term>Supernal Beings</term>—its direct rays—and Humanity. The grand Pantheistic ideal—of the unknown and unknowable Essence being transformed first into subjective and then into objective matter—is at the root of all these triads and triplets. Thus, we find in philosophical Northern Buddhism: (1) <term>Âdi-Buddha</term> (or Primordial Universal Wisdom); (2) the <term>Dhyâni-Buddhas</term> (or <term>Bodhisattvas</term>); and (3) the <term>Mânushi</term> (Human) Buddhas. In European conceptions, we find the same: God, Angels, and Humanity, symbolized theologically by the God-Man. The Brahmanical *Trimûrti* and also the threefold body of <term>Shiva</term> in Shaivism have both been conceived on the same basis, if they do not run entirely on the lines of Esoteric teachings.

Hence, it is no wonder if one finds this conception of the triple body—or the vestures of <term>Nirmânakâya</term>, <term>Sambhogakâya</term>, and <term>Dharmakâya</term>, the grandest of the doctrines of Esoteric Philosophy—accepted in a more or less disfigured form by every religious sect and explained quite incorrectly by the Orientalists. Thus, in its general application, the threefold body symbolizes Buddha’s statue, his teachings, and his <term>stûpas</term>; in the priestly conceptions, it applies to the Buddhist profession of faith called the *Triratna*, which is the formula of taking "refuge in Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha." 

Popular imagination makes Buddha ubiquitous, placing him thereby on a par with an anthropomorphic god and lowering him to the level of a tribal deity; as a result, it falls into flat contradictions, as seen in Tibet and China. Thus, the exoteric doctrine seems to teach that while in his <term>Nirmânakâya</term> body (which passed through 100,000 *kotis* of transformations on earth), Buddha is at the same time a <term>Lochana</term> (a heavenly <term>Dhyâni-Bodhisattva</term>) in his <term>Sambhogakâya</term> "robe of absolute completeness" and in <term>Dhyâna</term> (a state which must cut him off from the world and all its connections); and finally and lastly, besides being a <term>Nirmânakâya</term> and a <term>Sambhogakâya</term>, he is also a <term>Dharmakâya</term> "of absolute purity," a <term>Vairotchana</term> or <term>Dhyâni-Buddha</term> in full <term>Nirvâna</term>! (See Eitel’s *Sanskrit-Chinese Dictionary*.) 

This is the jumble of irreconcilable contradictions presented by missionaries and certain Orientalists as the *philosophical* dogmas of Northern Buddhism. If this is not an intentional confusion of a philosophy dreaded by those who uphold a religion based on inescapable contradictions and guarded "mysteries," then it is the product of ignorance. As the <term>Trailokya</term>, the <term>Trikâya</term>, and the <term>Triratna</term> are the three aspects of the same concept and must be, so to speak, blended into one, the subject is further explained under each of these terms. (See also the related term "<term>Tri-sharana</term>.")

**Trilochana (*Sk.*)**. *Literally*, "three-eyed," a title of <term>Shiva</term>. The story is told that while the god was engaged one day in strict spiritual disciplines on a Himalayan summit, his wife lovingly placed her hand over his eyes; immediately, a third eye burst from <term>Shiva's</term> forehead with a great flame. This is the eye that burned <term>Kâma</term>, the *god of love* (acting as <term>Mârâ</term>, the tempter), to ashes for trying to distract him with thoughts of his wife during his devotional meditation.

**Trimûrti (*Sk.*)**. *Literally*, "three faces," or "triple form"—the Trinity. In the modern pantheon, these three persons are <term>Brahmâ</term>, the creator; <term>Vishnu</term>, the preserver; and <term>Shiva</term>, the destroyer. However, this is a later development, as in the *<term>Vedas</term>* neither <term>Brahmâ</term> nor <term>Shiva</term> are known. The Vedic trinity consists of <term>Agni</term>, <term>Vâyu</term>, and <term>Sûrya</term>; or as the *<term>Nirukta</term>* explains it: the terrestrial fire, the atmospheric (or aerial) fire, and the heavenly fire, since <term>Agni</term> is the god of fire, <term>Vâyu</term> is the god of the air, and <term>Sûrya</term> is the sun. As the *<term>Padma Purâna</term>* describes it:

> "In the beginning, the great <term>Vishnu</term>, desiring to create the whole world, became triple: creator, preserver, and destroyer. To produce this world, the Supreme Spirit emerged from the right side of his body as <term>Brahmâ</term>; then, to preserve the universe, he produced <term>Vishnu</term> from the left side of his body; and to destroy the world, he produced the eternal <term>Shiva</term> from the middle of his body. Some worship <term>Brahmâ</term>, some <term>Vishnu</term>, others <term>Shiva</term>; but <term>Vishnu</term>, being one yet triple, creates, preserves, and destroys; therefore, let the devout make no distinction between the three."

The fact is that all three "persons" of the <term>Trimûrti</term> are simply the three qualifying <term>gunas</term> or attributes of the universe of differentiated Spirit-Matter—self-forming, self-preserving, and self-destroying—for the purposes of regeneration and reaching perfection. This is the correct meaning. It is shown in <term>Brahmâ</term> being made the personified embodiment of <term>Rajoguna</term>, the attribute of activity and the desire for procreation—the desire by which the universe and everything in it is brought into existence. <term>Vishnu</term> is the embodied <term>Sattvaguna</term>, that property of preservation arising from quietude and restful enjoyment which characterizes the middle period between full growth and the beginning of decay. Meanwhile <term>Shiva</term>, being the embodied <term>Tamaguna</term>—which is the attribute of stagnation and final decay—naturally becomes the destroyer. This concept is as deeply philosophical beneath its mask of personification as it is unphilosophical and absurd to believe in and impose the literal interpretation of the original concept upon the world.

**Tripada** (*Sk.*). “Three-footed,” fever, personified as having three feet or stages of development—cold, heat, and sweat.

**Tripitaka** (*Sk.*). *Literally*, “three baskets”; the name of the Buddhist canon. It is composed of three divisions: (1) the doctrine; (2) the rules and laws for the priesthood and ascetics; (3) the philosophical dissertations and metaphysics: namely, the <term>Abhidharma</term>, defined by <term>Buddhaghosa</term> as that law (<term>dharma</term>) which goes beyond (<term>abhi</term>) the law. The <term>Abhidharma</term> contains the most profoundly metaphysical and philosophical teachings, and is the storehouse from which the <term>Mahâyâna</term> and <term>Hînayâna</term> Schools got their fundamental doctrines. There is a fourth division—the *Samyakta Pitaka*. But as it is a later addition by the Chinese Buddhists, it is not accepted by the Southern Church of Siam and Ceylon.

**Triratna**, or *Ratnatraya* (*Sk.*). The Three Jewels, the technical term for the well-known formula “<term>Buddha</term>, <term>Dharma</term>, and <term>Sangha</term>” (or <term>Samgha</term>), the two latter terms meaning, in modern interpretation, “religious law” (<term>Dharma</term>), and the “priesthood” (<term>Sangha</term>). Esoteric Philosophy, however, would regard this as a very loose rendering. The words “<term>Buddha</term>, <term>Dharma</term>, and <term>Sangha</term>,” should be pronounced as in the days of <term>Gautama</term>, the Lord <term>Buddha</term>—namely “<term>Bodhi</term>, <term>Dharma</term>, and <term>Sangha</term>”; and interpreted to mean “Wisdom, its laws and priests,” the latter in the sense of “spiritual exponents,” or adepts. <term>Buddha</term>, however, being regarded as personified “<term>Bodhi</term>” on earth, a true avatar of <term>Âdi-Buddha</term>, <term>Dharma</term> gradually came to be regarded as his own particular law, and <term>Sangha</term> as his own special priesthood. Nevertheless, it is the uninitiated of the later (now modern) teachings who have shown a greater degree of natural intuition than the actual interpreters of <term>Dharma</term>, the Buddhist priests. The people see the <term>Triratna</term> in the three statues of <term>Amitâbha</term>, <term>Avalokiteshvara</term>, and <term>Maitreya Buddha</term>; that is, in “Boundless Light” or Universal Wisdom, an impersonal principle which is the correct meaning of <term>Âdi-Buddha</term>; in the “Supreme Lord” of the <term>Bodhisattvas</term>, or <term>Avalokiteshvara</term>; and in <term>Maitreya Buddha</term>, the symbol of the terrestrial and human Buddha, the “<term>Mânushi Buddha</term>.” Thus, even though the uninitiated do call these three statues “the Buddhas of the Past, the Present, and the Future,” still every follower of true philosophical Buddhism—called “atheistical” by Mr. Eitel—would explain the term <term>Triratna</term> correctly. The philosopher of the <term>Yogâchârya</term> School would say—as well he could—“<term>Dharma</term> is not a person but an unconditioned and underived entity, combining in itself the spiritual and material principles of the universe, while from <term>Dharma</term>

...proceeded, by emanation, Buddha [or rather, 'reflected' Bodhi], as the creative energy which produced, in conjunction with Dharma, the third factor in the trinity, namely, 'Samgha', which is the comprehensive sum total of all real life." Samgha, then, is not and cannot be what it is now understood to be—namely, the actual "priesthood"—for the latter is not the sum total of all *real* life, but only of religious life. The true primitive significance of the word Samgha or "Sangha" applies only to the Arhats, Bhikshus, or the "initiates"; that is to say, the real exponents of Dharma—the divine law and wisdom—which comes to them as a reflected light from the one "boundless light." This is its philosophical meaning. And yet, far from satisfying the scholars of the West, this seems only to irritate them; for E. J. Eitel, of Hong Kong, remarks on the above: "Thus the dogma of a Triratna, originating from three primitive articles of faith, and at one time culminating in the conception of three persons—a trinity in unity—has degenerated into a metaphysical theory of the evolution of three abstract *principles*"! And if one of the most capable European scholars will sacrifice every philosophical ideal to gross anthropomorphism, then what can Buddhism, with its subtle metaphysics, expect at the hands of ignorant missionaries?

**Trisharana (Sk.)**. The same as "Triratna" and accepted by both the Northern and Southern Churches of Buddhism. After the death of the Buddha, it was adopted by the councils as a mere kind of formula of faith (*formula fidei*), enjoining one "to take refuge in Buddha," "to take refuge in Dharma," and "to take refuge in Sangha," or his Church in the sense in which it is now interpreted; but it is not in this sense that the *Light of Asia* would have taught the formula. Of Trikâya, Mr. E. J. Eitel, of Hong Kong, tells us in his *Handbook of Chinese Buddhism* that this "trichotomy was taught regarding the nature of all Buddhas. Bodhi being the characteristic of a Buddha"—a distinction was made between "essential Bodhi" as the attribute of the Dharmakâya (the "essential body"); "reflected Bodhi" as the attribute of Sambhogakâya; and "practical Bodhi" as the attribute of Nirmânakâya. Buddha, by combining these three conditions of existence in himself, was said to live in three different spheres at the same time. Now, this shows how greatly the purely pantheistic and philosophical teaching is misunderstood. Without stopping to inquire how even a Dharmakâya vesture can have any "attribute" in Nirvâna—a state which is shown in philosophical Brahmanism as much as in Buddhism to be absolutely devoid of any attribute as conceived by finite human thought—it will be sufficient to point to the following: (1) the Nirmânakâya vesture is preferred by the "Buddhas of Compassion" over the Dharmakâya state, precisely because the latter prevents whoever attains it from any communication or relation with the finite world—that is, with humanity; (2) it is not Buddha (Gautama, the mortal man, or any other personal Buddha) who lives everywhere in "three different spheres at the same time," but Bodhi—the universal and abstract principle of divine wisdom, symbolized in philosophy by Âdi-Buddha. It is the latter that is present everywhere.

It is Bodhi, or the Spirit of Buddhaship, which is what is meant by the name "essential Bodhi"—having resolved itself into its primordial homogeneous essence and merged into it, just as Brahmâ (the universe) merges into Parabrahm, the <term>ABSOLUTENESS</term>. For the Nirvanee, or Dhyâni-Buddha, must be understood—by living in Arûpadhâtu, the formless state, and in Dharmakâya—to be that "essential Bodhi" itself. It is the Dhyâni Bodhisattvas, the primordial rays of the universal Bodhi, who live in "reflected Bodhi" in Rûpadhâtu, or the world of subjective "forms"; and it is the Nirmânakâyas (plural) who, upon ceasing their lives of "practical Bodhi" in the "enlightened" or Buddha forms, remain voluntarily in the Kâmadhâtu (the world of desire), whether in objective forms on earth or in subjective states in its sphere (the second Buddhakshetra). They do this in order to watch over, protect, and help humanity. Thus, it is neither one Buddha who is meant, nor any particular avatar of the collective Dhyâni Buddhas, but truly <term>Âdi-Bodhi</term>—the first Logos, whose primordial ray is Mahâbuddhi, the Universal Soul, <term>ALAYA</term>, whose flame is everywhere, and whose influence has a different sphere in each of the three forms of existence, because, once again, it is *Universal Being itself* or the reflection of the absolute. Hence, while it is philosophical to speak of Bodhi, which "as Dhyâni Buddha rules in the domain of the spiritual" (the fourth Buddhakshetra or region of Buddha); and of the Dhyâni Bodhisattvas "ruling in the third Buddhakshetra" or the domain of ideation; and even of the Mânushi Buddhas, who are in the second Buddhakshetra as Nirmânakâyas—to apply the "idea of a unity in trinity" to three personalities is highly unphilosophical.

**Trishnâ** (Sanskrit). The fourth Nidâna; spiritual love.

**Trishûla** (Sanskrit). The trident of Shiva.

**Trisuparna** (Sanskrit). A certain portion of the Veda; after thoroughly studying this, a Brâhman is also called a Trisuparna.

**Trithemius.** An abbot of the Spanheim Benedictines, a very learned Kabbalist and adept in the Secret Sciences, who was the friend and instructor of Cornelius Agrippa.

**Triton** (Greek). The son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, whose body from the waist upward was that of a man and whose lower limbs were those of a dolphin. Triton belongs, in esoteric interpretation, to the group of fish symbols—such as Oannes (Dagon), the *Matsya* or Fish-avatar, and the *Pisces*, as adopted in Christian symbolism. The dolphin is a constellation called *Capricornus* by the Greeks, and the latter is the Indian *Makâra*. It thus has an anagrammatic significance, and its interpretation is entirely occult and mystical, known only to advanced students of Esoteric Philosophy. Suffice it to say that it is as physiological as it is spiritual and mystical. (See *Secret Doctrine* II., pp. 578 and 579.)

**Trividyâ** (*Sk.*). Literally, “the three knowledges” or “sciences.” These are the three fundamental axioms in mysticism:—(*a*) the impermanence of all existence, or *Anitya*; (*b*) the suffering and misery of all that lives and exists, or *Dukha*; and (*c*) all physical, objective existence as evanescent and unreal as a water bubble in a dream, or *Anâtmâ*.

**Trivikrama** (*Sk.*). An epithet of Vishnu used in the *Rig Veda* in relation to the “three steps of Vishnu.” The first step he took on earth, in the form of Agni; the second in the atmosphere, in the form of Vâyu, god of the air; and the third in the sky, in the shape of Sûrya, the sun.

**Triyâna** (*Sk.*). “The three vehicles” across Sansâra—the ocean of births, deaths, and rebirths—are the vehicles called Shravaka, Pratyeka Buddha, and Bodhisattva, or the three degrees of yogic mastery. The term Triyâna is also used to denote the three schools of mysticism—the Mahâyâna, Madhyimâyâna, and Hînayâna schools; of which the first is the “Greater,” the second the “Middle,” and the last the “Lesser” Vehicle. All systems between the Greater and the Lesser Vehicles are considered “useless.” Therefore, the Pratyeka Buddha is made to correspond with the Madhyimâyâna. For, as explained, “this (the Pratyeka Buddha state) refers to him who lives all for himself and very little for others, occupying the middle of the vehicle, filling it all and leaving no room for others.” Such is the selfish candidate for Nirvâna.

**Tsanagi-Tsanami** (*Jap.*). A kind of creative god in Japan.

**Tsien-Sin** (*Chin.*). The “Heaven of Mind,” Universal Ideation and Mahat, when applied to the plane of differentiation: “Tien-Sin” (see entry) when referring to the Absolute.

**Tsien-Tchan** (*Ch.*). The universe of form and matter.

**Tsi-tsai** (*Chin.*). The “Self-Existent” or the “Unknown Darkness,” the root of Wuliang Sheu, “Boundless Age,” all Kabbalistic terms which were used in China ages before the Hebrew Kabbalists adopted them, borrowing them from Chaldea and Egypt.

**Tubal-Cain** (*Heb.*). The Biblical Kabir, “an instructor of every craftsman in brass and iron,” the son of Zillah and Lamech; one with the Greek Hephaestus or Vulcan. His brother Jubal, the son of Adah and the brother (from the same mother) of Jabal—one the father of those “who handle the harp and organ,” and the other the father “of those who have cattle”—are also Kabiri. For, as shown by Strabo, it is the Kabiri (or Cyclopes in one sense) who made the harp for Kronos and the trident for Poseidon, while some of their other brothers were instructors in agriculture. Tubal-Cain (or Thubal-Cain) is a word used in the Master Mason’s degree in the ritual and ceremonies of the Freemasons.

**Tullia** (*Lat.*). A daughter of Cicero, in whose tomb, as claimed by several alchemists, was found burning a perpetual lamp, placed there more than a thousand years previously.

**Tum, or Toom.** The "Brothers of the Tum," a very ancient school of Initiation in Northern India during the days of Buddhist persecution. The "Tum B’hai" have now become the "Aum B’hai," though spelled differently at present, as both schools have merged into one. The first was composed of <term>Kshatriyas</term>, and the second of <term>Brahmans</term>. The word "Tum" has a double meaning: that of darkness (absolute darkness), which as an absolute is higher than the highest and purest of lights; and a meaning based on the mystical greeting among Initiates, "Thou art thou, yourself," which is equivalent to saying "You are one with the Infinite and the All."

**Turîya** (*Sk.*). A state of the deepest trance—the fourth state of the <term>Târaka Râja Yoga</term>, which corresponds with <term>Âtmâ</term>, and on this earth with dreamless sleep—a causal condition.

**Turîya Avasthâ** (*Sk.*). Almost a <term>Nirvânic</term> state in <term>Samâdhi</term>, which is itself a beatific state of the contemplative <term>Yoga</term> beyond this plane. It is a condition of the higher Triad, quite distinct (though still inseparable) from the conditions of <term>Jagrat</term> (waking), <term>Svapna</term> (dreaming), and <term>Sushupti</term> (sleeping).

**Tushita** A class of gods of great purity in the Hindu Pantheon. In exoteric or popular Northern Buddhism, it is a <term>Deva-loka</term>, a celestial region on the material plane where all the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> are reborn before they descend to this earth as future Buddhas.

**Tyndarus** (*Gr.*). King of <term>Lacedæmon</term>, the fabled husband of <term>Leda</term>, the mother of <term>Castor</term> and <term>Pollux</term> and of <term>Helen of Troy</term>.

**Typhæus** (*Gr.*). A famous giant who had a hundred heads like those of a serpent or dragon, and who was the reputed father of the Winds, just as <term>Siva</term> was the father of the <term>Maruts</term>—who are also "winds." He made war against the gods and is identical with the Egyptian <term>Typhon</term>.

**Typhon** (*Eg.*). An aspect or shadow of <term>Osiris</term>. <term>Typhon</term> is not, as Plutarch asserts, the distinct "Evil Principle" or the Satan of the Jews; but rather the lower cosmic "principles" of the divine body of <term>Osiris</term>, the god within them—<term>Osiris</term> being the personified universe as an ideation, and <term>Typhon</term> as that same universe in its material realization. The two in one are <term>Vishnu</term>-<term>Siva</term>. The true meaning of the Egyptian myth is that <term>Typhon</term> is the terrestrial and material envelope of <term>Osiris</term>, who is the indwelling spirit of it. In chapter 42 of the *Ritual* ("Book of the Dead"), <term>Typhon</term> is described as "<term>Set</term>, formerly called <term>Thoth</term>." Orientalists find themselves greatly perplexed to discover <term>Set</term>-<term>Typhon</term> addressed in some papyri as "a great and good god," and in others as the embodiment of evil. But is not <term>Siva</term>, one of the Hindu <term>Trimûrti</term>, described in some places as "the best and most bountiful of gods," and at other times as "a dark, black, destroying, terrible" and "fierce god"? Did not <term>Loki</term>, the Scandinavian <term>Typhon</term>, after having been described in earlier times as a beneficent being—as the god of fire and the presiding genius of the peaceful domestic hearth—suddenly lose status and immediately become a power of evil, a cold-hell Satan and a demon of the worst kind? There is a good reason for such an invariable transformation. So long

However, as soon as they are separated into two entities, each with its own characteristics, they become respectively the two opposite poles of good and evil, of light and darkness; in short, they become two independent and distinct entities, or rather personalities. It is only by means of sophistry that the Churches have succeeded to this day in preserving the Jewish deity in his primeval integrity in the minds of a few. Had they been logical, they would have separated Christ from Jehovah—light and goodness from darkness and badness. And this is what happened to Osiris-Typhon; but no Orientalist has understood it, and thus their confusion continues to increase. Once accepted—as the Occultists do—as an integral part of Osiris (just as Ahriman is an inseparable part of Ahura Mazda, and the Serpent of Genesis is the dark aspect of the Elohim, blended into our “Lord God”), every difficulty regarding the nature of Typhon disappears.

Typhon is a later name for Set—later, yet still ancient, dating back as far as the Fourth Dynasty; for in the *Ritual* one reads: 
> “O Typhon-Set! I invoke you, terrible, invisible, all-powerful god of gods, you who destroy and turn the land into a desert.”

Typhon belongs most decidedly to the same symbolic category as Shiva <note>Spelled "Siva" in the original text.</note> the Destroyer, and Saturn—the “dark god.” In the *Book of the Dead*, Set, in his battle with Thoth (wisdom)—who is his spiritual counterpart—is emasculated just as Saturn-Kronos was, and Uranus <note>Spelled "Ouranos" in the original text.</note> before him.

Just as Shiva is closely connected with the bull Nandi—an aspect of Brahma-Vishnu, the creative and preserving powers—so is Set-Typhon allied with the bull Apis; both bulls are sacred to and associated with their respective deities.

As Typhon was originally worshiped as an upright stone, the phallus, so Shiva is represented and worshiped to this day as a lingam. Shiva is Saturn. Indeed, Typhon-Set seems to have served as a prototype for more than one god of the later ritualistic cycle, including even the god of the Jews; some of his ritualistic observances passed entirely into the code of laws and the canon of religious rites of the “chosen people.”

Who among the Bible-worshipers knows the origin of the scapegoat (*ez* or *aza*) sent into the wilderness as an atonement? Do they know that ages before the exodus of Moses, the goat was sacred to Typhon, and that it was over the head of that Typhonic goat that the Egyptians confessed their sins, after which the animal was released into the desert? 
> “And Aaron shall take the scapegoat (*Azazel*) . . . and lay his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel . . . and shall send him away . . . into the wilderness” (*Leviticus*, 16).

And as the goat of the Egyptians made an atonement with Typhon, so the goat of the Israelites 
> “made an atonement before the Lord” (*Ibid.*, v. 10).

# THEOSOPHICAL

Mazda and Ahriman, etc., etc.—it will be easy for the reader to comprehend the assertion made by the Occultists that Typhon was but a symbol for the lower quaternary, the ever-conflicting and turbulent principles of differentiated chaotic matter, whether in the Universe or in Man, while Osiris symbolized the higher spiritual triad. Typhon is accused in the Ritual of being one who "steals reason from the soul." Hence, he is shown fighting with Osiris and cutting him into fourteen (twice seven) pieces, after which—left without his counterbalancing power of good and light—he remains steeped in evil and darkness. In this way, the fable told by Plutarch becomes comprehensible as an allegory. He asserts that, overcome in his fight with Horus, Typhon "fled seven days on an ass, and escaping begat the boys Ierosolumos and Ioudaios." Now, as Typhon was worshipped at a later period under the form of an ass, and as the name of the ass is AO, or (phonetically) IAO—the vowels mimicking the braying of the animal—it becomes evident that Typhon was purposely blended with the name of the Jewish God, as the two names of Judea and Jerusalem, fathered by Typhon, sufficiently imply.

**Twashtri** (*Sk.*). The same as Vishwakarman, "the divine artist," the carpenter and weapon-maker of the gods. (See "Vishwakarman.")

**Tzaila** (*Heb.*). A rib; see *Genesis* for the myth of the creation of the first woman from a rib of Adam, the first man. It is curious that no other myth describes anything like this "rib" process, except the Hebrew Bible. Other similar Hebrew words are "Tzela, a 'fall'," and Tzelem, "the image of God." Inman remarks that the ancient Jews were fond of punning wordplay, and sees one here—that Adam *fell* on account of a *woman* whom God made in his *image*, from a *fall* in the man's side. <note>W.W.W.</note>

**Tzelem** (*Heb.*). An image, a shadow. The shadow of the physical body of a man, also the astral body—*Linga Sharîra*. (See "Tzool-mah".)

**Tzim-tzum** (*Kab.*). Expansion and contraction, or, as some Kabbalists explain it—"the centrifugal and centripetal energy."

**Tziruph** (*Heb.*). A set of combinations and permutations of the Hebrew letters, designed to show analogies and preserve secrets. For example, in the form called Atbash, A and T were substitutes, B and Sh, G and R, etc. <note>W.W.W.</note>

**Tzool-mah** (*Kab.*) *Lit.*, "shadow." It is stated in the *Zohar* (I., 218 *a*, 1. fol. 117 *a*, col. 466.), that during the last seven nights of a man's life, the *Neshamah*—his spirit—leaves him, and the shadow, *tzool-mah*, acts no longer, his body casting no shadow; and when the *tzool-mah* disappears entirely, then *Ruach* and *Nephesh*—the soul and life—go with it. It has been often urged that in Kabbalistic philosophy there were but three, and, with the Body (*Guff*), four "principles." It can be easily shown there are seven, and several subdivisions more, for there are the "upper" and the "lower" *Neshamah* (the dual *Manas*); *Ruach*, Spirit or *Buddhi*; *Nephesh* (*Kâma*) which "has no light from her own substance," but is associated with the *Guff*, Body; and *Tzelem*, "Phantom of the Image";

**<term>Tzuphon</term>** (*Hebrew*). A name for Boreas, the north wind, which some of the ancient Israelites deified and worshipped.

**<term>Tzurah</term>** (*Hebrew*). The divine prototype in the *Kabbalah*. In Occultism, it encompasses <term>Âtmâ-Buddhi-Manas</term>, the highest triad; the eternal divine *individual*. The plural is <term>tzurath</term>.

**<term>Tzure</term>** (*Hebrew*). The Jewish Occultists knew of no single Adam and, refusing to recognize humanity and its Adam as the first human race, spoke only of "primordial sparks".

# U.

**U.**—The twenty-first letter of the Latin alphabet, which has no equivalent in Hebrew. As a number, however, it is considered very mystical both by the Pythagoreans and the Kabbalists, as it is the product of 3 x 7. The latter consider it the most sacred of the old numbers, as 21 is the sum of the numerical value of the Divine Name *aeie*, or *eiea*, or again *aheihe*—thus (read backward, *aheihe*):
->he i he a<-
->5+10+5+1=21.<-
In Alchemy it symbolizes the twenty-one days necessary for the transmutation of base metals into silver.

**Uasar** (*Eg.*). The same as Osiris, the latter name being Greek. Uasar is described as the "Egg-born," like Brahmâ. "He is the egg-sprung Eros of Aristophanes, whose creative energy brings all things into existence; the demiurge who made and animates the world, a being who is a sort of personification of Amen, the invisible god, as Dionysos is a link between mankind and the Zeus Hypsistos" (*The Great Dionysiak Myth*, Brown). Isis is called Uasi, as she is the <term>Sakti</term> of Osiris, his female aspect, both symbolizing the creating, energizing, vital forces of nature in its aspect of male and female deity.

**Uchchaih-Sravas** (*Sk.*). The model-horse; one of the fourteen precious things or jewels produced at the Churning of the Ocean by the gods. The white horse of Indra, called the Râjâ of horses.

**Uchanîcha**, also **Buddhôchnîcha** (*Sk.*). Explained as "a protuberance on Buddha's cranium, forming a hair-tuft." This curious description is given by the Orientalists, varied by another which states that Uchnîcha was "originally a conical or flame-shaped hair tuft on the crown of a Buddha, in later ages represented as a fleshy excrescence on the skull itself." This ought to read quite the reverse; for esoteric philosophy would say: Originally an orb with the *third eye* in it, which degenerated later in the human race into a fleshy protuberance, to disappear gradually, leaving in its place but an occasional flame-colored aura, perceived only through clairvoyance, and when the exuberance of spiritual energy causes the (now concealed) "third eye" to radiate its superfluous magnetic power. At this period of our racial development, it is of course the "Buddhas" or Initiates alone who enjoy in full the faculty of the "third eye," as it is more or less atrophied in everyone else.

**Udâna** (*Sk.*). Extemporaneous speeches; also Sûtras. In philosophy the term applies to the physical organs of speech, such as tongue, mouth,

**Udayana** (*Sk.*). Modern Peshawer. "The classic *land of sorcery*," according to Hiouen-Thsang.

**Udayana Râjâ** (*Sk.*). A King of Kausâmbî, called Vatsarâjâ, who was the first to have a statue of Buddha made before his death; in consequence of which—say the *Roman Catholics*, who build statues of Madonnas and Saints at every street corner—he "*became the originator of* BUDDHIST IDOLATRY."

**Udra Ramaputra** (*Sk.*). Udra, the son of Râma. A Brahman ascetic who was the Guru of Gautama Buddha for some years.

**Udumbara** (*Sk.*). A lotus of gigantic size, sacred to Buddha: the *Nila Udumbara* or "blue lotus," regarded as a supernatural omen whenever it blossoms, for it flowers only once every three thousand years. One such, it is said, burst forth before the birth of Gautama; another appeared near a lake at the foot of the Himalayas in the fourteenth century, just before the birth of Tsong-kha-pa, etc., etc. The same is said of the Udumbara tree (*Ficus glomerata*) because it flowers at intervals of long centuries, as does also a kind of cactus which blossoms only at extraordinary altitudes and opens at midnight.

**Ullambana** (*Sk.*). The festival of "all souls," the prototype of All Souls' Day in Christian lands. It is held annually in China during the *seventh moon*, when both "Buddhist and Taoist priests read masses to release the souls of those who died on land or sea from purgatory, scatter rice to feed Prêtas <note>thirty-six classes of demons who are ever hungry and thirsty</note>, consecrate domestic ancestral shrines, . . . recite Tantras . . . accompanied by magic finger-play (mûdra) to comfort the ancestral spirits of seven generations in Nâraka" (a kind of purgatory or *Kâma Loka*). The author of the *Sanskrit-Chinese Dictionary* thinks that this is the old Tibetan (Bhon) "*Gtorma* ritual grafted onto Confucian ancestral worship," due to Dharmaraksha translating the *Ullambana Sûtra* and introducing it into China. This Sûtra is certainly a forgery, as it presents these rites on the authority of Sâkyamuni Buddha and "supports it by the alleged experiences of his principal disciples, Ânanda being said to have appeased Prêtas by food offerings." But as correctly stated by Mr. Eitel, "the whole theory, with the ideas of intercessory prayers, priestly litanies and requiems, and ancestral worship, is entirely foreign to ancient and Southern Buddhism." And to the Northern too, if we except the sects of Bhootan and Sikkim, of the Bhon or Dugpa persuasion—the *red caps*, in short. As the ceremonies of All Saints' Day, or days, are known to have been introduced into China in the third century (265-292), and as the same Roman Catholic ceremonial and ritual for the dead, held on November 2nd, did not exist in those early days of Christianity, it cannot be the Chinese who bor-

**Uller** (*Scand.*). The god of archery, who “journeys over the silvery ice-ways on skates.” He is the patron of the chase during the period when the Sun passes over the constellation of <term>Sagittarius</term>; he lives in the “Home of the Light-Elves,” which is in the Sun and outside of <term>Asgard</term>.

**Ulom** (*Phœnic.*). The intelligible deity. The objective or material <term>Universe</term>, in the theogony of <term>Mœchus</term>. The reflection of the ever-concealed deity; the <term>Plêrôma</term> of the <term>Gnostics</term>.

**Ulphilas** (*Scand.*). A scholar who created a new alphabet for the <term>Goths</term> in the fourth century—a combination of <term>Greek</term> letters with the form of the <term>runic alphabet</term>. From that time, the runes began to die out and their secret was gradually lost. (See “Runes”.) He translated the <term>Bible</term> into <term>Gothic</term>, which is preserved in the *<term>Codex Argenteus</term>*.

**Ulûpî** (*Sk.*). A daughter of <term>Kauravya</term>, King of the *<term>Nâgas</term>* in *<term>Pâtâla</term>* (the underworld, or more correctly, the <term>Antipodes</term>, <term>America</term>). Exoterically, she was the daughter of a king or chief of an aboriginal tribe of the *Nâgas*, or *<term>Nâgals</term>* (ancient adepts) in prehistoric <term>America</term>—most likely <term>Mexico</term>, or perhaps <term>Uruguay</term>. She was married to <term>Arjuna</term>, the disciple of <term>Krishna</term>, whom every tradition, oral and written, describes as traveling five thousand years ago to Pâtâla (the Antipodes). The <term>Purânic</term> tale is based on a historical fact. Moreover, the name <term>Ulûpî</term> has a <term>Mexican</term> sound to it, similar to “<term>Atlan</term>,” “<term>Alco</term>,” etc.

**Umâ-Kanyâ** (*Sk.*). *Lit.,* “<term>Virgin of Light</term>”; a title unsuitable for its possessor, as it was that of <term>Durgâ Kâlî</term>, the goddess or female aspect of <term>Siva</term>. Human flesh was offered to her every autumn; and, as <term>Durgâ</term>, she was the patroness of the once murderous <term>Thugs of India</term>, and the special goddess of <term>Tântrika sorcery</term>. But in ancient times, it was not as it is now. The earliest mention of the title “Umâ-Kanyâ” is found in the *<term>Kena-Upanishad</term>*; in it, the now bloodthirsty <term>Kâlî</term> was a benevolent goddess, a being of light and goodness who brings about reconciliation between <term>Brahmâ</term> and the gods. She is <term>Saraswatî</term> and she is <term>Vâch</term>. In <term>esoteric symbology</term>, Kâlî is the dual type of the dual soul—the divine and the human, the light and the dark soul of man.

**Umbra** (*Lat.*). The shadow of an earth-bound <term>spook</term>. The ancient <term>Latin races</term> divided man (in esoteric teachings) into <term>seven principles</term>, as did every old system, and as <term>Theosophists</term> do now. They believed that after death *<term>Anima</term>*, the pure divine soul, ascended to heaven, a place of bliss; *<term>Manes</term>* (the *<term>Kâma Rûpa</term>*) descended into <term>Hades</term> (*<term>Kâma Loka</term>*); and *<term>Umbra</term>* (or the astral double, the *<term>Linga Sharîra</term>*) remained on earth, hovering about its tomb, because the attraction of physical, objective matter and affinity to the physical body kept it within the places which that body had impressed with its emanations. **Una** (*Sk.*). Something underlying; subordinate; secondary also, and material.

**Undines** (*Lat.*). Water nymphs and spirits. One of the four principal kinds of elemental spirits, which are *Salamanders* (fire), *Sylphs* (air), *Gnomes* (earth), and *Undines* (water).

**Upâdâna** (*Sk.*). Material Cause; as flax is the cause of linen.

**Upâdâna Kâranam** (*Sk.*). The material cause of an effect.

**Upâdhi** (*Sk.*). Basis; the vehicle, carrier, or bearer of something less material than itself: as the human body is the *upâdhi* of its spirit, ether the *upâdhi* of light, etc.; a mold; a defining or limiting substance.

**Upadvîpas** (*Sk.*). The root (underlying) of islands; dry land.

**Upanishad** (*Sk.*). Translated as “esoteric doctrine,” or interpretation of the Vedas by the *Vedânta* methods. The third division of the Vedas appended to the *Brâhmanas* and regarded as a portion of *Sruti* or “revealed” word. They are, however, as records, far older than the *Brâhmanas*—with the exception of the two still extant attached to the *Rig-Veda* of the Aitareyins. The term *Upanishad* is explained by the Hindu pundits as “that which destroys ignorance, and thus produces liberation” of the spirit, through the knowledge of the supreme though hidden truth; the same, therefore, as that which was hinted at by Jesus, when he is made to say, “And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (*John* viii. 32). It is from these treatises of the *Upanishads*—themselves the echo of the primeval Wisdom-Religion—that the *Vedânta* system of philosophy has been developed. (See “*Vedânta*”.) Yet old as the *Upanishads* may be, the Orientalists assign to the oldest of them an antiquity of no more than 600 years <term>B.C.</term> The accepted number of these treatises is 150, though now no more than about twenty are left unadulterated. They treat of very abstruse, metaphysical questions, such as the origin of the Universe; the nature and the essence of the Unmanifested Deity and the manifested gods; the connection, primal and ultimate, of spirit and matter; the universality of mind and the nature of the human Soul and Ego.

The *Upanishads* must be far more ancient than the days of Buddhism, as they show no preference for, nor do they uphold, the superiority of the Brahmans as a caste. On the contrary, it is the (now) second caste, the Kshatriya, or warrior class, who are exalted in the oldest of them. As stated by Professor Cowell in Elphinstone’s *History of India*—“they breathe a freedom of spirit unknown to any earlier work except the *Rig-Veda*. . . . The great teachers of the higher knowledge and Brahmans are continually represented as going to Kshatriya Kings to become their pupils.” The “Kshatriya Kings” were in the olden times, like the King-Hierophants of Egypt, the receptacles of the highest divine knowledge and wisdom, the Elect and the incarnations of the primordial divine Instructors—the Dhyâni Buddhas or Kumâras. There was a time, eons

**Upanita** (*Sk.*). One who is invested with the Brahmanical thread; literally, “brought to a spiritual teacher or Guru.”

**Uparati** (*Sk.*). Absence of outgoing desire; a Yoga state.

**Upâsaka** (*Sk.*). Male chelas or rather devotees. Those who, without entering the priesthood, vow to preserve the principal commandments.

**Upâsika** (*Sk.*). Female chelas or devotees.

**Upasruti** (*Sk.*). According to Orientalists, a “*supernatural voice which is heard at night revealing the secrets of the future*.” According to the explanation of Occultism, it is the voice of any person at a distance—generally one versed in the mysteries of esoteric teachings or an adept—endowed with the gift of projecting both his voice and astral image to any person whatsoever, regardless of distance. The *upasruti* may “reveal the secrets of the future,” or may only inform the person it addresses of some prosaic fact of the present; yet it will still be an *upasruti*—the “double” or the echo of the voice of a living man or woman.

**Upekshâ** (*Sk.*). Literally, Renunciation. In Yoga, a state of absolute indifference attained by self-control, the complete mastery over one’s mental and physical feelings and sensations.

**Ur** (*Chald.*). The chief seat of lunar worship; the Babylonian city where the moon was the chief deity, and from where Abraham brought the Jewish god, who is so inextricably connected with the moon as a creative and generative deity.

**Uræus** (*Gr.*). In Egyptian *Urhek*, a serpent and a sacred symbol. Some see in it a cobra, while others say it is an asp. Cooper explains that “*the asp is not a uræus but a cerastes, or kind of viper, i.e., a two-horned viper. It is the royal serpent, wearing the pschent . . . the naga hâje*.” The uræus is “round the disk of Horus and forms the ornament of the cap of Osiris, besides overhanging the brows of other divinities” (Bonwick). Occultism explains that the uræus is the symbol of initiation and also of hidden wisdom, as the serpent always is. The gods were all patrons of the hierophants and their instructors.

**Urâgas** (*Sk.*). The Nâgas (serpents) dwelling in Pâtâla, the nether world or hell, in popular thought; the Adepts, High Priests and Initiates of Central and South America, known to the ancient Aryans; where Arjuna wedded the daughter of the king of the Nâgas—Ulûpi. Nagalism or Nâga-worship prevails to this day in Cuba and Haiti, and Voodooism in New Orleans. In Mexico the chief “*sorcerers*,” the “*medicine men*,” are called Nagals.

to this day; just as thousands of years ago the Chaldean and Assyrian High Priests were called *Nâgals*, as they were the chiefs of the Magi (*Rab-Mag*), an office held at one time by the prophet Daniel. The word *Nâga*, "wise serpent," has become universal because it is one of the few words that has survived the wreck of the first universal language. In South as well as in Central and North America, the indigenous peoples use the word, from the Bering Straits down to Uruguay, where it means a "chief," a "teacher," and a "serpent." The very word *Uraga* may have reached India and been adopted through its connection, in prehistoric times, with South America and Uruguay itself, for the name belongs to the American Indian vernacular. The origin of the Uragas, for all that Orientalists know, may have been in Uruguay, as there are legends about them which locate their ancestors, the Nâgas, in *Pâtâla*—the antipodes, or America.

**Uranides** (*Gr.*). One of the names of the *divine* Titans, those who rebelled against Kronos, the prototypes of the Christian "fallen" angels.

**Urim** (*Heb.*). See "Thummim." The "Urim and Thummim" originated in Egypt and symbolized the *Two Truths*, with the two figures of *Ra* and *Thmei* being engraved on the breastplate of the Hierophant and worn by him during the initiation ceremonies. Diodorus adds that this gold necklace with precious stones was worn by the High Priest when delivering judgment. *Thme* (plural *Thmin*) means "Truth" in Hebrew. "The Septuagint translates thummim as 'Truth'" (Bonwick). The late Mr. Proctor, the astronomer, shows that the Jewish idea was "derived directly from the Egyptians." But Philo Judaeus affirms that Urim and Thummim were "the two small images of Revelation and Truth, put between the double folds of the breastplate," and he passes over the latter, with its twelve stones typifying the twelve signs of the Zodiac, without explanation.

**Urlak** (*Scand.*). The same as "Orlog" (*q.v.*). Fate; an impersonal power bestowing gifts "blindly" on mortals; a kind of Nemesis.

**Urvasî** (*Sk.*). A divine nymph, mentioned in the *Rig-Veda*, whose beauty set the whole heaven ablaze. Cursed by the gods, she descended to earth and settled there. The loves of Purûravas (the Vikrama) and the nymph Urvasî are the subject of Kâlidâsa’s world-famous drama, the *Vikramorvasî*.

**Usanas** (*Sk.*). The planet Venus or Sukra; or rather the ruler and governor of that planet.

**Ushas** (*Sk.*). The dawn, the daughter of heaven; the same as the Aurora of the Latins and the ἠώς of the Greeks. She is first mentioned in the Vedas, where her name is also *Ahanâ* and *Dyotanâ* (the illuminator), and she is a most poetical and fascinating image. She is the ever-faithful friend of humans, of both the rich and the poor, though she is believed to prefer the latter. She smiles upon and visits the dwelling of every living mortal. She is the immortal, ever-youthful virgin, the light of the poor, and the destroyer of darkness.

# V.

**V.**—The twenty-second letter of the Latin alphabet. Numerically, it stands for 5; hence the Roman V̅ (with a dash) stands for 5,000. Western Kabbalists have connected it with the divine Hebrew name IHVH. However, since the Hebrew *Vau* is number 6, it is only by being identical with the W that it can ever become a proper symbol for the male-female and spirit-matter. The equivalent for the Hebrew *Vau* is YO, and in numerals, it is 6.

**Vâch** (*Sk.*). To call Vâch simply “speech” lacks clarity. Vâch is the mystic personification of speech and the female *Logos*, being one with Brahmâ, who created her out of one-half of his body, which he divided into two portions; she is also one with Virâj (called the “female” Virâj) who was created within her by Brahmâ. In one sense, Vâch is “speech” by which knowledge was taught to man; in another, she is the “mystic, secret speech” which descends upon and enters into the primeval Rishis, just as the “tongues of fire” are said to have “sat upon” the apostles. For she is called “the female creator,” the “mother of the Vedas,” etc. Esoterically, she is the subjective Creative Force which, emanating from the Creative Deity (the subjective Universe, its “privation,” or ideation), becomes the manifested “world of speech”—that is, the concrete expression of ideation, hence the “Word” or *Logos*. Vâch is “the male and female” Adam of the first chapter of *Genesis*, and is thus called “Vâch-Virâj” by the sages (See *Atharva Veda*). She is also “the celestial Saraswatî produced from the heavens,” a “voice derived from speechless Brahmâ” (*Mahâbhârata*); the goddess of wisdom and eloquence. She is called *Sata-rûpa*, the goddess of a hundred forms.

**Vacuum** (*Lat.*). Esoterically, the symbol of the absolute Deity or Boundless Space.

**Vâhana** (*Sk.*). A vehicle; the carrier of something immaterial and formless. All the gods and goddesses are, therefore, represented as using *vâhanas* to manifest themselves, and these vehicles are always symbolic. So, for instance, during *Pralayas*, Vishnu has *Ananta* “the infinite” (Space), symbolized by the serpent *Sesha*; and during the *Manvantaras*, he has *Garuda*, the gigantic half-eagle, half-man, the symbol of the great cycle. Brahmâ appears as Brahmâ, descending into the planes of manifestation on *Kâlahamsa*, the “swan in time or finite eternity”; Siva (pronounced *Shiva*) appears as the bull *Nandi*; Osiris as the sacred bull *Apis*; Indra travels on an elephant; Kârttikeya on a peacock; Kâmadeva on *Makâra*, and at other times a parrot; Agni, the universal (and also solar) Fire-god, who is, as all of them are, “a consuming Fire,” manifests

**Vaibhâchikas** (*Sk.*). The followers of the *Vibhâcha Shâstra*, an ancient school of materialism; a philosophy that held that no mental concept can be formed except through direct contact between the mind and external objects via the senses, such as sight, touch, taste, etc. There are *Vaibhâchikas* in India to this day.
**Vaidhâtra** (*Sk.*). The same as the *Kumâras*.
**Vaidyuta** (*Sk.*). Electric fire, the same as *Pâvaka*, one of the three fires which, when divided, produce forty-nine mystic fires.
**Vaihâra** (*Sk.*). The name of a cave-temple near *Râjâgriha*, where the Lord *Buddha* usually retired for meditation.
**Vaijayantî** (*Sk.*). The magic necklace of *Vishnu*, imitated by certain Initiates among the temple *Brahmans*. It is made of five precious stones, each symbolizing one of the five elements of our Round; namely, the pearl, ruby, emerald, sapphire, and diamond, or water, fire, earth, air, and ether, called “the aggregate of the five elemental rudiments”—the word “powers” being, perhaps, more correct than “rudiments.”
**Vaikhari Vâch** (*Sk.*). That which is uttered; one of the four forms of speech.
**Vaikuntha** (*Sk.*). One of the names of the twelve great gods, from which comes *Vaikunthaloka*, the abode of *Vishnu*.
**Vairâjas** (*Sk.*). In popular belief, these are semi-divine beings, the shades of saints, unconsumable by fire and impervious to water, who dwell in *Tapo-loka* with the hope of being moved to *Satya-loka*—a more purified state which corresponds to *Nirvâna*. The term is explained as the aerial bodies or astral shades of “ascetics, mendicants, anchorites, and penitents, who have completed their course of rigorous austerities.” In esoteric philosophy, they are called *Nirmânakâya*; *Tapo-loka* is on the sixth plane (upward) but in direct communication with the mental plane. The *Vairâjas* are referred to as the first gods because the *Mânasa-putras* and the *Kumâras* are the oldest in theogony; it is said that even the gods worshipped them (*Matsya Purâna*). They are those whom *Brahmâ*, “with the eye of Yoga, beheld in the eternal spheres, and who are the gods of gods” (*Vâyu Purâna*).
**Vairochana** (*Sk.*). “All-enlightening.” A mystic symbol, or rather a generic personification of a class of spiritual beings described as the embodiment of essential wisdom (*bodhi*) and absolute purity. They dwell in the fourth *Arûpa Dhâtu* (formless world) or *Buddhakshetra*, and are the first or the highest hierarchy of the five orthodox *Dhyâni Buddhas*. There was a *Sramana* (an *Arhat*) of this name (see *Eitel’s Sansk. Chin. Dict.*), a native of *Kashmir*, “who introduced *Buddhism* into *Kustan* and labored in *Tibet*” (in the seventh century of our era). He was the best translator of the semi-esoteric Canon of Northern *Buddhism*, and a contemporary of the great *Samantabhadra* (see entry).

**Vaisâkha** (*Sk.*). A celebrated female ascetic, born at Shravasti, and called *Sudatta*, "virtuous donor." She was the mother-abbess of a Vihara, or convent of female Upasikas, and is known as the builder of a Vihara for Shakyamuni Buddha. She is regarded as the patroness of all the Buddhist female ascetics.

**Vaisheshika** (*Sk.*). One of the six *Darshanas* or schools of philosophy, founded by Kanada. It is called the Atomistic School, as it teaches the existence of a universe of atoms of a temporary nature, an endless number of souls, and a fixed number of material principles. Through the correlation and interaction of these, periodic cosmic evolutions take place without any directing force, except for a kind of mechanical law inherent in the atoms; it is a very materialistic school.

**Vaishnava** (*Sk.*). A follower of any sect recognizing and worshiping Vishnu as the one supreme God. The worshipers of Shiva are called *Shaivas*.

**Vaivaswata** (*Sk.*). The name of the Seventh Manu, the forefather of the post-flood race, or our own fifth humankind. A reputed son of Surya (the Sun), he became—after having been saved in an ark (built by the order of Vishnu) from the Great Flood—the father of Ikshwaku, the founder of the solar race of kings. (See "Suryavansa".)

**Vajra** (*Sk.*). *Literally*, "diamond club" or scepter. In Hindu works, it is the scepter of Indra, similar to the thunderbolts of Zeus, with which this deity, as the god of thunder, slays his enemies. But in mystical Buddhism, it is the *magic* scepter of Priest-Initiates, exorcists, and adepts—the symbol of the possession of *Siddhis* or superhuman powers, wielded during certain ceremonies by the priests and theurgists. It is also the symbol of Buddha's power over evil spirits or elementals. The possessors of this wand are called *Vajrapani* (*q.v.*).

**Vajrâchârya** (*Sk.*). The spiritual *acharya* (*guru*, *teacher*) of the Yogacharyas. The "Supreme Master of the Vajra."

**Vajradhara** (*Sk.*). The Supreme Buddha according to the Northern Buddhists.

**Vajrapâni** (*Sk.*), or *Manjushri*, the Dhyani-Bodhisattva (as the spiritual reflection, or the son of the Dhyani-Buddhas, on earth) born directly from the subjective form of existence; a deity worshiped by the uninitiated as a god, and by Initiates as a subjective force, the real nature of which is known only to, and explained by, the highest Initiates of the Yogacharya School.

**Vajrasattva** (*Sk.*). The name of the sixth Dhyani-Buddha (of whom there are only *five* in popular Northern Buddhism)—in the Yogacharya school, the latter counts seven Dhyani-Buddhas and as many Bodhisattvas, the "mind-sons" of the former. Hence, the Orientalists refer to Vajrasattva as "a fictitious Bodhisattva."

**Vallabâchârya** (*Sk.*). The name of a mystic who was the *chela* (disciple) of Vishnu Swami, and the founder of a sect of Vaishnavas. His

**Vâmana** (*Sk.*). The fifth avatar of Vishnu; hence the name of the Dwarf whose form was assumed by that god.

**Vara** (*Mazd.*). A term used in the *Vendîdâd*, where Ahura-mazda commands Yima to build *Vara*. It also signifies an enclosure or vehicle, an ark (*argha*), and at the same time MAN (verse 30). *Vara* is the vehicle of our informing Egos—that is, the human body—the soul in which is typified by the expression a "window self-shining within".

**Varâha** (*Sk.*). The boar-avatar of Vishnu; the third in number.

**Varna** (*Sk.*). Caste; *literally*, "colour". The four chief castes named by Manu—the Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaisya, and Sûdra—are called *Chatur-varna*.

**Varsha** (*Sk.*). A region, a plain; any stretch of country situated between the great mountain ranges of the earth.

**Varuna** (*Sk.*). The god of water, or marine god, but far different from Neptune; for in the case of this oldest of the Vedic deities, *Water* means the "Waters of Space", or the all-investing sky, *Âkâsa*, in one sense. Varuna or *Ooaroona* (phonetically), is certainly the prototype of the *Ouranos* of the Greeks. As Muir says: "The grandest cosmic functions are ascribed to Varuna. Possessed of illimitable knowledge . . . . he upholds heaven and earth, he dwells in all worlds as sovereign ruler. . . . . He made the golden . . . . sun to shine in the firmament. The wind which resounds through the atmosphere is his breath. . . . Through the operation of his laws the moon walks in brightness and the stars . . . . mysteriously vanish in daylight. He knows the flight of birds in the sky, the paths of ships on the ocean, the course of the far-traveling wind, and beholds all the things that have been or shall be done. . . . . He witnesses men's truth and falsehood. He instructs the Rishi Vasishta in mysteries; but his secrets and those of Mitra are not to be revealed to the foolish." . . . . "The attributes and functions ascribed to Varuna impart to his character a moral elevation and sanctity far surpassing that attributed to any other Vedic deity."

**Vasishta** (*Sk.*). One of the primitive seven great Rishis, and a most celebrated Vedic sage.

**Vasudeva** (*Sk.*). The father of Krishna. He belonged to the Yâdava branch of the *Somavansa*, or lunar race.

**Vasus** (*Sk.*). The eight evil deities attendant upon Indra. Personified cosmic phenomena, as their names show.

**Vâyu** (*Sk.*). Air: the god and sovereign of the air; one of the five states of matter, namely the *gaseous*; one of the five elements, called, as wind, *Vâta*. The *Vishnu Purâna* makes Vâyu King of the Gandharvas. He is the father of Hanumân, in the *Râmâyana*. The trinity of the
